question: Is standing at a desk for part of the workday actually better for health than sitting, and how large is the measured effect?

scopeContract.decisionAtStake: Two purchase/policy decisions, each with a real price tag. (1) Individual: spend roughly $150-600 (converter) to $600-1,500 (full electric sit-stand desk) in 2026 USD and restructure the workday around posture changes. (2) Employer/HR: fund sit-stand desks fleet-wide at roughly $400-900 per head, versus spending the same budget on walking-meeting/movement-break policy, an ergonomics assessment program, or subsidized exercise — versus doing nothing. The framing of the answer also changes who pays and on what grounds: if standing produces health-grade benefit, it is a wellness/occupational-health line item defensible on outcome data; if it produces only comfort and small surrogate-marker shifts, it is a preference/amenity purchase that should not carry a health claim, and org-level rollout loses its justification while individual purchase may still be fine. A reader who concludes "it's basically neutral for health but cheap and people like it" acts very differently from one who concludes "this measurably lowers cardiometabolic risk."
scopeContract.keyQuestion: For a healthy adult desk worker, does replacing roughly 2-4 hours per day of sitting with standing produce health benefits large enough — on cardiometabolic markers, musculoskeletal pain, or hard endpoints — to justify the cost of a sit-stand setup, or is the measured effect small enough that the money and behavior change belong elsewhere (walking breaks, structured exercise)?
assumptions: Population: healthy working-age (roughly 20-65) office workers in high-income countries, sedentary >6 h/workday. Excludes pregnancy, existing chronic venous insufficiency or varicose veins, prior lumbar surgery, and people already on their feet for work.

Exposure of interest: INTERMITTENT standing of ~2-4 h across an 8-h workday, alternating with sitting. This is deliberately NOT the same exposure as occupational prolonged standing (retail, nursing, assembly line, 6-8 h near-continuous). The occupational-standing cohorts that report elevated CVD and varicose-vein risk will be used only as an upper-bound harm signal, never as the effect estimate for desk workers — conflating the two is the single most common error in this literature and I am ruling it out up front.

Comparator: the same person sitting the whole workday, holding leisure-time exercise constant. Treadmill desks and walking pads are OUT of the primary scope but tracked separately, because they are the key discriminator for whether posture or ambulation is the active ingredient.

Outcome hierarchy, ranked: (a) hard endpoints — all-cause and CVD mortality, incident type 2 diabetes; (b) validated intermediates — systolic BP, HbA1c, fasting insulin/HOMA-IR, postprandial glucose iAUC, waist circumference, LDL/triglycerides; (c) musculoskeletal — low back and neck/shoulder pain; (d) secondary — fatigue, mood, self-reported productivity, plus harms (lower-limb swelling, orthostatic symptoms, foot pain).

Time horizon: effects that persist at 6-24 months. Short crossover lab studies (single-day postprandial) count as mechanism evidence only, not as the effect estimate. I assume no RCT with mortality endpoints exists or will exist, so hard-endpoint evidence will be observational and confounded.

Thresholds for 'large', set before looking: systolic BP drop >=3 mmHg, HbA1c >=0.3%, waist circumference >=2 cm, low back pain >=2 points on 0-10 or >=30% relative (standard MCID), and a durable objectively-measured sitting reduction >=60 min/workday. 'Small' is a real but sub-MCID effect; 'null' is a CI comfortably spanning zero at >=6 months.

Evidence weighting: device-measured (accelerometer/inclinometer) exposure over self-report, which systematically over-reports standing; RCTs and cluster-RCTs over pre-post; >=6-month follow-up over <=3-month; and I will discount trials where the sit-stand desk arrived bundled with coaching, prompts, or a movement campaign, since those confound the desk with the co-intervention.
Costs in 2026 USD; primarily US/UK/AU/Nordic evidence base, where most of the sit-stand trial literature (Stand Up Victoria, SMArT Work, Take-a-Stand) originates.

'Better than sitting' is interpreted as a within-person substitution effect at constant total exercise — not as 'standers are healthier than sitters,' which is largely a confounded cross-sectional claim.
whatWouldChangeTheAnswer: A >=12-month RCT with device-measured sitting showing BOTH a durable sitting reduction and cardiometabolic improvement exceeding the MCIDs above — this would promote the answer from 'small/comfort' to 'health-grade intervention.'

Evidence that the sitting reduction achieved by sit-stand desks decays toward baseline (<30 min/day) by 12 months. If the behavior doesn't stick, the effect size question is moot regardless of mechanism, and the purchase decision fails on adherence alone.

Isolation trials that hold step count constant between arms: if the benefit survives, posture itself is active (supports H1/H2); if it vanishes, the desk is a proxy for movement and the money should go to walking breaks (supports H3).

Large device-measured prospective cohorts (e.g. UK Biobank accelerometer analyses) showing standing time flat or adverse for CVD while stepping time is protective — a direct strike against the standing-specific benefit story and toward H3/H4.

A dose-response harm signal appearing WITHIN the 2-4 h/day intermittent range (orthostatic hypotension, venous disease, incident low back pain in previously asymptomatic standers) rather than only at 6+ h continuous — this would flip the recommendation to a capped, structured protocol or against standing.

Evidence that the surrogate-to-hard-outcome chain is broken at these magnitudes — i.e., that postprandial glucose or small BP changes of this size have not translated to event reduction in trials that tested them — which downgrades any 'improves markers' finding to H2.

Pain results running opposite to the health results: several trials report standing desks help low back pain while doing little metabolically, and some report standing INDUCING back pain in a susceptible subgroup. A strong, replicated musculoskeletal benefit could justify the purchase even if the metabolic answer is null — and a harm signal could sink it even if metabolism improves.

Cost data: if converters at ~$150 make the outlay trivial, even a small (H2) effect clears the bar for individuals while still failing to justify a mandated org-wide rollout. The cost figure and the effect size have to be read together, not sequentially.

hypotheses.hypothesis: H1 — Health-grade benefit: intermittent standing of 2-4 h/day produces improvements that clear the pre-set MCIDs on validated intermediates (BP, glycemic control, waist circumference) and is plausibly linked to reduced cardiometabolic risk, independent of leisure exercise. Sit-stand desks are a genuine health intervention.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Pooled >=6-month RCT evidence with device-measured exposure shows intermediate-marker changes that are null or sub-MCID (e.g. systolic BP <3 mmHg, HbA1c <0.3%), AND device-measured cohorts show no dose-response between standing time and CVD/mortality after adjustment for MVPA and stepping. Either half being solidly negative demotes H1 to H2; both negative kills it outright.

hypotheses.hypothesis: H2 — Real but small: standing yields modest, mostly sub-MCID improvements on surrogate markers, a modest reduction in low back/neck discomfort, and better subjective energy — enough to be worth a cheap desk on comfort-plus-marginal-health grounds, but not enough to be called a health intervention or to justify an employer health claim.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Killed upward if effects on any tier-(b) intermediate exceed MCID and replicate at >=6 months (becomes H1). Killed downward if meta-analyzed discomfort and marker effects are null with CIs spanning zero at >=6 months once co-intervention-confounded trials are excluded (becomes H3). H2 survives only in the awkward middle, so I need effect sizes with intervals, not p-values.

hypotheses.hypothesis: H3 — Posture is not the active ingredient: standing per se is roughly neutral; what benefits health is BREAKING UP sedentary time with muscle activity and ambulation. Sit-stand desks appear to work in trials only because they prompt movement or arrive bundled with movement coaching. The correct purchase is a walking-break habit, not a desk.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Trials that isolate posture — standing arms with step counts matched to seated controls, or lab crossovers substituting standing-only (no ambulation) for sitting — still show postprandial glycemic or BP benefit versus sitting. A clean posture-isolated positive result kills H3.

hypotheses.hypothesis: H4 — Net neutral-to-harmful at meaningful doses: standing buys no cardiometabolic benefit and carries offsetting costs — lower-limb venous pooling, orthostatic circulatory risk, foot and low-back discomfort — with harms rising as standing time increases, meaning the honest advice is to move more, not stand more, and to cap standing duration.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Large device-measured cohorts and >=6-month trials show no elevated incidence of venous disease, orthostatic events, or new-onset low back pain at intermittent 2-4 h/day exposures, with any harm signal confined to the 6+ h near-continuous occupational range. Absence of a harm dose-response inside the decision-relevant exposure window kills H4.

answerFirst: On the evidence that survived verification, standing for part of the workday is not shown to be better for health than sitting — it is shown to be *achievable*. A sit-stand desk plus coaching reliably converts about one hour of daily sitting into standing and holds most of it at 12 months with walking unchanged, but the measured health return on that posture swap is small and imprecise where positive (postprandial glucose, Cohen's d = -0.31, upper CI bound -0.03), and null for insulin, systolic blood pressure, short-term musculoskeletal symptoms, and incident major cardiovascular disease; the single favourable hard-endpoint signal comes from women of median age 80 and is markedly stronger when the standing includes walking.
hingeNumber: The hinge is Cohen's d = -0.31 (95% CI -0.60 to -0.03) for postprandial glucose from standing breaks — the only positive, posture-isolated, pooled effect in the whole surviving set (Buffey et al., Sports Medicine 2022, 7 acute 1-day crossover trials). If it is wrong by a factor of two in standing's favour (d ≈ -0.62), standing becomes a moderate acute metabolic intervention and the answer flips toward "yes, meaningfully better." If it is wrong by half (d ≈ -0.15), standing is indistinguishable from null and the answer hardens to "no measurable benefit from posture alone" — and note that d = -0.15 already sits *inside* the reported confidence interval, whereas d = -0.62 sits outside it. The interval is therefore asymmetric against standing: the downside case is supported by the paper's own numbers, the upside case is not. A secondary hinge is the achieved dose, 63.7 min/day of sitting displaced (95% CI -80.1 to -47.4) in the best RCT; double it and trials would finally be testing above the 2.6 h/day threshold at which the only cross-sectional cardiometabolic association appears, halve it and the intervention is trivial.
baseRate: The evidence contains event base rates only for populations that are not the one the question is about. UK Biobank accelerometer cohort: 6,829 major CVD events among 75,897 adults over a mean 6.9 years (≈9% cumulative, ≈1.3%/year — arithmetic on the confirmed figures, an inference not a stated rate). WHI OPACH: 691 deaths in 5,878 women over 26,649 person-years (mean 4.8 y), with crude all-cause mortality running 34.8 down to 21.3 deaths per 1,000 person-years across ascending quartiles of standing without ambulation, and 50.0 down to 11.5 for standing with ambulation. There is NO base rate in this evidence for the decision-relevant population — working-age office workers — on any hard endpoint, and none at all for musculoskeletal injury incidence, venous events, or new-onset pain at desk standing doses. One trial is not a base rate, and neither is one cohort of octogenarian women.
strongestArgumentAgainst: The crux of the question is untested, and my "no demonstrated benefit" reading may be an artefact of under-dosing plus wrong endpoints. Every RCT here delivers roughly one hour per day of extra standing — 74.4 min during work hours at 3 months decaying to 58.8 min at 12 months — while the only dose-response analysis in the set (Ahmadi et al., Diabetologia 2024) reports that a minimum of 2.6 h/day of standing is required before more favourable cardiometabolic health appears. If that threshold is real, then every null in this report is a null at roughly 40% of the required dose, and absence of measured benefit is not evidence of absence of benefit. Second, the null endpoints are short-horizon surrogates: the pooled glucose/insulin/SBP result comes from *one-day* crossover trials, and the Cochrane musculoskeletal null rests on two RCTs at under six months rated low-quality — that is an absence of demonstrated benefit from a thin evidence base, not demonstrated absence. Third, the one study in this set with a hard endpoint and adequate follow-up (OPACH, 691 deaths, 26,649 person-years) found standing *without* ambulation associated with 37% lower all-cause mortality after adjustment for accelerometer-measured MVPA, in a dose-response gradient across all four quartiles (p-trend = .003), with the result robust to excluding first-year deaths. An informed opponent would say: the UK Biobank CVD null is a different endpoint in a different population, and I am privileging a null over a dose-responsive, confounder-adjusted mortality association because the null is more convenient. Fourth, and most damaging to any confident verdict in *either* direction: the adversarial panel killed roughly 30 claims including several that would have loaded the anti-standing side (the orthostatic/venous harm signal above 2 h/day, the walking-beats-standing head-to-heads, the 24-month cardiometabolic nulls, the cost-effectiveness findings). This report is therefore not a balanced ledger — it is the residue of what survived, and the harm side of the ledger was pruned harder than the benefit side.
whatWouldChangeThisCall: A working-age, device-measured cohort in which standing time predicts lower all-cause mortality after mutual adjustment for stepping and MVPA. That single result would adjudicate the OPACH-vs-UK-Biobank tension in standing's favour and move the answer from 'unproven' to 'probably yes'.

An RCT that actually sustains 2.6+ h/day of standing (above the Ahmadi threshold) for 6-12 months with a step-count-matched control, reporting BP, HbA1c, lipids and waist against established MCIDs. Every trial in this set tops out near one hour/day, so this is the experiment that has not been run.

A larger or updated meta-analysis of acute crossover trials whose glucose confidence interval excludes small effects — i.e. a pooled d whose upper bound is well clear of zero, or conversely one that crosses zero. The current interval (-0.60 to -0.03) is compatible with both 'worthwhile' and 'nothing', and tightening it either way resolves the hinge.

Pooled musculoskeletal effect sizes at 3 and 6 months on a validated scale benchmarked against an MCID, plus a credible incidence estimate for venous/orthostatic harms at intermittent 2-4 h/day desk doses. Demonstrated harm inside the decision window would flip the answer to net-negative regardless of the glycemic result; a clean comfort benefit would justify the desk on non-metabolic grounds.
summary: A height-adjustable desk plus a behaviour-change programme does what it says on the tin behaviourally: 63.7 min/day less device-measured sitting versus control at 12 months (95% CI -80.1 to -47.4), of which 41.7 min/day is attributable to the desk itself over the identical programme delivered without one, with work-hours standing up 74.4 min at 3 months and 58.8 min at 12 months and stepping essentially unchanged — a near-pure posture substitution of about one hour. The health return on that substitution is where the case thins out: pooled across seven acute crossover trials, standing breaks cut postprandial glucose by only d = -0.31 (95% CI -0.60 to -0.03) with no significant effect on insulin or systolic blood pressure, and one controlled lab study found continuous standing across a 2-hour OGTT raised lower-body EMG while not reducing glucose at all versus sitting inactive. In the largest device-measured cohort (75,897 adults, 6,829 events, 6.9 years) standing time showed no association with major CVD, while sitting above 10 h/day carried an HR increase of 0.15 per extra hour — pointing the benefit, if any, at sitting reduction rather than at standing itself. Cochrane found no significant reduction in low back (SMD -0.35, 95% CI -0.80 to 0.10) or upper back symptom intensity (SMD -0.48) from sit-stand workstations under six months, both low-quality evidence, and the best RCT blood-pressure result (DBP -2.24 mmHg; SBP -3.33 mmHg, which missed the trial's own prespecified alpha of P<0.025) belongs to a sit-to-stand *transition* arm in postmenopausal women, not to standing time. The one favourable hard endpoint — all-cause mortality 37% lower in the top quartile of standing without ambulation among 5,878 women of median age 80 — is both population-remote from desk work and outperformed by standing that includes walking (HR 0.50 vs 0.63). The honest verdict: the behaviour is deliverable and durable to 12 months, the health effect of the posture change alone is small, imprecise, or unmeasured, and the question of whether it is "better than sitting" is not settled by this evidence.

findings.claim: A sit-stand desk plus a behaviour-change programme reliably converts about one hour of daily sitting into standing and retains roughly four-fifths of that at 12 months — but one hour is the ceiling the best trial achieves, and the desk (not the coaching) is what delivers it.
findings.evidence: SMART Work & Life, 78-cluster/756-participant three-arm cluster RCT with activPAL measurement. Daily sitting at 12 months: desk arm -63.7 min/day vs control (95% CI -80.1 to -47.4, P<0.001); identical programme without a desk only -22.2 min/day (95% CI -38.8 to -5.7, P=0.003); the desk's marginal contribution -41.7 min/day (95% CI -56.3 to -27.0, P<0.001). Work-hours standing rose 74.4 min at 3 months (95% CI 58.7 to 89.9) and 58.8 min at 12 months (95% CI 45.1 to 72.5), a decay of ~16 min (~21%) but still far above a 30 min/day floor. The behaviour-only arm produced no significant standing increase at either timepoint (4.7 min at 3 months, 13.0 min at 12 months, both CIs crossing zero). No 24-month data exist — the follow-up was removed because of covid-19.
findings.sourceTier: T1 (PMC full text, peer-reviewed BMJ cluster RCT)
findings.citationCheck: supported — three separate blind audits confirmed every effect size, CI and P value verbatim against the paper's abstract and Table 3, plus the covid-19 protocol-change sentence. One noted imprecision: Table 3's unit is min/work hours, not min/day, so the work-hours standing figures are not per-day figures (the paper's whole-day standing effect is 47.2 min at 3 months and 39.0 at 12 months).
findings.vote: 2-1 on each of the three constituent claims

findings.claim: Standing substituted for sitting produces only a small and imprecise acute glycemic benefit and no measurable effect on insulin or systolic blood pressure; at least one controlled lab protocol found zero glucose benefit despite confirmed muscle activation.
findings.evidence: Pooled across seven acute, 1-day randomised crossover trials in mixed-sex adults (predominantly overweight/obese): "standing as an interruption to prolonged sitting significantly reduced postprandial glucose (∆ = -0.31, 95% CI -0.60, -0.03; z = -2.15, p < 0.04) but had no significant effect on insulin or SBP." The ∆ is the paper's own Cohen's d. The upper CI bound of -0.03 sits practically at null, so the effect is small by convention and imprecise. Independently corroborating the null direction, the iScience limitations section reports: "One well-designed study reported that although standing continuously over a 2-h OGTT can raise EMG in the large muscles of the lower body, it did not reduce glucose at all compared with sitting inactive (Gao et al., 2017)."
findings.sourceTier: T? for both (doi.org resolvers; provenance independently confirmed via Crossref/Europe PMC to Sports Medicine 52(8):1765-1787 and iScience 25(9):104869 respectively)
findings.citationCheck: supported for both — verbatim abstract matches confirmed. Two flags carried forward: the Gao result is the iScience authors' second-hand characterisation of someone else's study, not their own data (the original should be pulled); and the meta-analysis tested *interrupting* prolonged sitting with standing bouts, not wholesale replacement of the sitting day.

findings.claim: In the largest device-measured cohort, standing time shows no association whatsoever with incident major cardiovascular disease, while sitting shows a clear dose gradient above 10 h/day.
findings.evidence: UK Biobank accelerometer sub-study, 75,897 adults in the CVD sample, 6,829 events, mean 6.9 ±0.9 years follow-up. "For major CVD, when stationary time exceeded 12 h/day, risk was higher by an average of 0.13 (0.10, 0.16) per hour. Sitting time was associated with a 0.15 (0.11, 0.19) higher risk per extra hour. Time spent standing was not associated with major CVD risk." Major CVD = coronary heart disease, heart failure and stroke. The sitting figure attaches to the >10 h/day range the paper's own conclusions specify.
findings.sourceTier: T1 (PMC full text, peer-reviewed prospective cohort)
findings.citationCheck: supported — abstract and results text matched verbatim; the CHD/HF/stroke gloss is the paper's own definition. IMPORTANT SCOPE FLAG raised by a verifier: the same paper separately reports standing above 2 h/day associated with higher *orthostatic circulatory disease* risk (0.11 [0.05, 0.18] per extra 30 min/day). The claims asserting that harm signal were REFUTED by the panel, so this report does not assert it — but the null above is scoped to major CVD only and must not be read as 'standing is harmless overall'.

findings.claim: The mechanism with the most cohort support is reducing sitting hours, not accumulating standing hours — which matters because the desk demonstrably delivers the former (about one hour) and the health value of the latter is unestablished.
findings.evidence: Reasoning, not a stated result: UK Biobank finds a monotone sitting-CVD gradient (+0.15 HR per hour above 10 h/day) with a flat standing-CVD line; the pooled acute trials find posture change alone worth only d = -0.31 on glucose and nothing on insulin or SBP; and SWAL shows the desk removes 63.7 min/day of sitting. If sitting hours are the exposure that carries risk, a desk that removes one sitting hour is doing something real even if 'standing' per se does nothing — but by the same logic any intervention that removes an equivalent sitting hour would do as much, and this evidence set does not contain the ≥6-month head-to-head comparators needed to test that.
findings.citationCheck: supported for each underlying claim individually; the synthesis is my reasoning and is not asserted by any source. Note that the panel REFUTED the claims characterising walking breaks as superior to standing breaks, so no comparator ranking is asserted here.
findings.vote: n/a — derived from claims voted 2-1, 2-1 and 2-1

findings.claim: The one favourable hard-endpoint association for standing comes from a cohort of women of median age 80, and within that cohort standing that includes walking carries a substantially larger signal than standing alone.
findings.evidence: WHI OPACH: 5,878 community-dwelling women (median age 80), one week of ActiGraph GT3X+ with validated machine-learning posture classification, 691 deaths over 26,649 person-years (mean 4.8 y). Fully adjusted (Model 3: age, race/ethnicity, education, self-rated health, chronic conditions, smoking, alcohol, physical function, BMI, and residualised MVPA minutes) — standing WITHOUT ambulation Q4 vs Q1 HR = 0.63 (95% CI 0.49-0.81), p-trend = .003; standing WITH ambulation Q4 vs Q1 HR = 0.50 (95% CI 0.35-0.71), p-trend < .001. Crude mortality per 1,000 person-years falls 34.8 → 21.3 across standing-alone quartiles versus 50.0 → 11.5 across standing-with-ambulation quartiles. Excluding first-year deaths left the pattern similar.
findings.sourceTier: T? (doi.org resolver; provenance independently confirmed to J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2021;76(1):77-84, PMC7756713)
findings.citationCheck: supported — every HR, CI, p-trend and crude rate matched verbatim against the abstract and results table, and the MVPA-adjustment qualifier was confirmed against the full text's Model 3 definition. Two flags: the paper does not formally test the two HRs against each other and their CIs overlap, so 'standing with ambulation is stronger' is descriptive, not inferential; and the paper itself states replication is required to determine generalisability to older men and younger age groups.

findings.claim: Every trial in this evidence set delivers standing well below the only dose at which a cardiometabolic association has been observed, so the nulls may be nulls at an under-dose — but that dose threshold is explicitly non-causal and cannot be used as a treatment target.
findings.evidence: Ahmadi et al. (ProPASS pooled thigh-worn accelerometry, Diabetologia 2024) identify a 2.6 h/day standing threshold for more favourable composite cardiometabolic health. The authors state plainly: "Our observational cross-sectional design limited inferences of causality, and influences of reverse causation may be present." All standing-cardiometabolic associations in that paper are cross-sectional; there is no prospective or interventional arm. Against that, SWAL's achieved work-hours standing increase is 74.4 min at 3 months and 58.8 min at 12 months — roughly 40% of 2.6 h/day. The under-dose reading is therefore arithmetically available but rests on a threshold that its own authors decline to treat as causal.
findings.citationCheck: supported — the limitations sentence and the 2.6 h/day figure were both confirmed verbatim on the PMC page, and the SWAL standing figures were confirmed against Table 3. NOTE: the panel REFUTED the claims characterising the *magnitude* of the effect at that threshold and the time-efficiency comparison against walking/stair-climbing, so neither is asserted here — only that the threshold exists and is non-causal.

findings.claim: The best randomised blood-pressure evidence belongs to sit-to-stand *transitions* in postmenopausal women, not to standing time — and its systolic half failed the trial's own prespecified significance threshold.
findings.evidence: Three-arm RCT (NCT03473145), 388 postmenopausal women completing 3 months, versus a healthy-living control arm: "The sit-to-stand arm had significant decreases in diastolic blood pressure compared with the healthy living arm (-2.24 mm Hg [95% CI, -4.08 to -0.40]; P=0.02) and similar decreases in systolic blood pressure compared with the healthy living arm (-3.33 mm Hg [95% CI, -6.32 to -0.33]; P=0.03), although it did not reach the a priori significance threshold of P<0.025." The trailing caveat attaches to the systolic result (P=0.03 > 0.025); diastolic clears it.
findings.sourceTier: T? (doi.org resolver; provenance independently confirmed to Circulation 152(8):492-504, 2025)
findings.citationCheck: supported — every figure matched the Crossref/Europe PMC abstract verbatim, including the a priori threshold clause, and the 'versus control' label matches the paper's own designation of healthy living as the control arm. Verifier flag carried forward: the intervention is increased sit-to-stand transitions in postmenopausal women, NOT desk standing, and this figure must not be restated as a general standing-desk effect.

findings.claim: Sit-stand workstations have not been shown to reduce musculoskeletal symptom intensity in the short term; the pooled estimates are non-significant and the evidence behind them is rated low-quality.
findings.evidence: Cochrane review (Parry et al., 2019), sit-stand workstations vs no intervention, short term (<6 months): "no significant difference in the intensity of low back symptoms (standardised mean difference (SMD) -0.35, 95% confidence interval (CI) -0.80 to 0.10; 2 RCTs; low-quality evidence) nor in the intensity of upper back symptoms (SMD -0.48, 95% CI -.096 to 0.00; 2 RCTs; low-quality evidence)." The upper-back CI is a published typesetting error; -0.96 to 0.00 is the only interval consistent with the -0.48 point estimate, and the PubMed rendering of the same abstract prints -.96. Both estimates rest on two RCTs each. This is an absence of demonstrated benefit on a thin, low-quality base, not demonstrated absence of benefit (that distinction is my inference).
findings.sourceTier: T3 (Cochrane Library URL returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch; content independently confirmed via Crossref and Europe PMC keyed to the identical DOI, PMID 31742666 / PMC6953379)
findings.citationCheck: supported — verbatim match including the anomalous '-.096', and the statement flags rather than hides the typo. Every qualifier (comparator, <6-month horizon, 2 RCTs, low-quality GRADE) survives intact.

findings.claim: A mechanistic pillar frequently invoked for sitting harm — inactivity-suppressed muscle lipoprotein lipase — rests, in this paper, entirely on rodents with no human participants, no device-measured posture exposure, and no clinical endpoints.
findings.evidence: Bey & Hamilton, J Physiol 551(2):673-682 (2003): "The robustness of the finding that physical inactivity significantly decreases muscle LPL activity was evident from confirmatory studies with different models of inactivity, in many rats and mice, both sexes, three muscle types and during both acute and chronic (11 days) treatment." A verifier confirmed the MeSH indexing for PMID 12815182 lists Animals, Mice, Rats but NOT Humans, and the sample is 166 female + 12 male Sprague-Dawley rats plus 12 female C57BL/6 mice; interventions are hindlimb unloading, tenotomy, actinomycin D and treadmill walking. Outcomes are molecular (LPL activity, mRNA, protein mass, triglyceride uptake), not clinical events. No retraction, erratum or expression of concern across 372 citing works.
findings.sourceTier: T? (doi.org resolver; provenance independently confirmed to J Physiol 551(2):673-682, PMC2343229)
findings.citationCheck: supported — the positive half matched the abstract clause-for-clause and the absence half was verified against MeSH indexing and the full text. Minor incompleteness noted and judged non-material: the paper also ran a 7-day continuous unloading arm alongside the 11-day intermittent protocol.

contradictions: HARD ENDPOINTS, UNRESOLVED: OPACH finds device-measured standing WITHOUT ambulation protective for all-cause mortality (Q4 vs Q1 HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.49-0.81, MVPA-adjusted, p-trend .003) in 5,878 women of median age 80; UK Biobank finds standing has NO association with incident major CVD in 75,897 working-age-inclusive adults. Both are device-measured and both adjust for ambulation, so they cannot both generalise. Candidate reconciliations nobody in this evidence set tests: different populations (octogenarian women vs general adults), different endpoints (all-cause mortality vs CVD incidence), and the possibility that OPACH's entire exposure range sits at low absolute standing volumes. Nothing here adjudicates.

ACUTE GLYCEMIA, UNRESOLVED: the pooled crossover meta-analysis reports a statistically significant glucose reduction from standing bouts (d = -0.31, 95% CI -0.60 to -0.03), while the Gao et al. 2017 lab protocol found zero glucose reduction across a 2-hour OGTT with continuous standing. A third pooled analysis (Henson et al. 2020) reportedly concluded neither glucose nor insulin is reduced by standing, but the claim asserting that was REFUTED by the panel and the primary paper was never pulled — so the adjudicating document is missing. Two pooled analyses over a largely overlapping acute literature apparently reach opposite signs on the same marker.

DOSE DURABILITY, PARTIALLY RESOLVED: SWAL shows work-hours standing decaying ~21% between 3 and 12 months but remaining substantial (58.8 min), with no 24-month data because covid-19 removed the follow-up. Other claims in the gathering phase asserted both sustained 2-year adherence and complete fade of benefits by 24 months; ALL of those were refuted or unverified, so this report can say nothing about what happens past 12 months. That is a gap, not a resolution.

BLOOD PRESSURE ATTRIBUTION, UNRESOLVED: the Circulation trial's blood-pressure benefit belongs to the sit-to-stand TRANSITION arm, not to a standing-time arm. If the active ingredient is the transition event rather than standing duration, a height-adjustable desk earns credit for an effect it does not deliver unless users actually transition frequently. The claims that would have settled this — on how often real-world desk owners actually change posture, and on how transitions dissociate from sitting volume — were both REFUTED, so the question is open.

BALANCE OF THE LEDGER: roughly 30 claims were killed by the adversarial panel, and they were disproportionately on the harm and comparator side — the orthostatic/venous harm signal above 2 h/day, the walking-beats-standing head-to-heads, the 24-month cardiometabolic nulls, the occupational-standing back-pain odds ratio, and every cost-effectiveness figure. This report is the residue of what survived, not a symmetric weighing, and readers should not treat the absence of a harm finding here as evidence of no harm.

Standing's association with hard endpoints: the OPACH cohort finds device-measured standing WITHOUT ambulation protective for all-cause mortality (Q4 vs Q1 HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.49-0.81, MVPA-adjusted), while the UK Biobank accelerometer cohort finds standing has NO association with incident CVD and is associated with HARM above ~2 h/day for orthostatic circulatory disease (+0.11 HR per extra 30 min/day), with the authors explicitly naming office standing desks as unlikely to achieve a cardiovascular goal. Both are device-measured and both mutually adjust for ambulation, so they cannot both generalize; the candidate reconciliations (median age 80 women vs working-age adults; mortality vs CVD/venous endpoints; only 0.9 h/d mean standing in OPACH, i.e. the whole exposure range sits BELOW the UK Biobank harm inflexion) are exactly what an adjudicating source needs to test.

Acute standing-vs-sitting glycemia: the pooled crossover meta-analysis reports a statistically significant reduction in postprandial glucose from standing bouts (Cohen's d = -0.31, 95% CI -0.60 to -0.03), while Henson et al. 2020, pooling four large postprandial laboratory studies, concluded neither glucose NOR insulin is decreased by standing, and Gao et al. 2017 found zero glucose reduction across a 2-hour OGTT with continuous standing. Two pooled analyses over a largely overlapping acute lab literature reach opposite signs on the same marker; the Henson 2020 primary paper is the adjudicating document and is currently only a second-hand characterization inside another paper.

Whether workplace sitting reduction reaches the 24-hour total: the 12-24 month follow-up concludes workers who stand at work do NOT compensate outside work, and the 18-24 month activPAL study found no significant change in leisure-time behavior; but the habitual-use activPAL study found workstation sitting time had NO relationship with total daily sitting time in the same population type, which is the signature of compensation elsewhere in the day. Either the workplace reduction survives into the daily total or it does not.

Durability of adherence: the 18-24 month activPAL follow-up reports workplace sitting still down 78-84 min/day at 2 years with no decay, and the 12-24 month study retains 23.5% of baseline reduction, while the habitual (non-trial) device-measured study finds real-world sit-stand desk owners change desk position only twice per day and still sit 39% of workstation time, and the 24-month RCT found all 6-month benefits fully faded. The n=10, no-control-arm, self-selected design of the sustained-adherence finding versus the free-living sample is the likely resolution, but as stated the claims conflict.

Blood pressure attribution: the coached RCT's sit-to-stand transition arm lowered SBP 3.33 mmHg and DBP 2.24 mmHg while total sitting time was statistically unchanged, whereas the compositional device-measured analysis (n=14,761) finds standing has 'minimal impact' on BP, needing ~78 min/day reallocation for 1 mmHg DBP and reaching NO clinically meaningful SBP change at any dose. These are reconcilable only if the active ingredient is the transition event rather than standing time - which, if true, means a sit-stand desk is being credited for an effect it does not deliver unless users actually transition frequently (and the habitual-use data says they transition twice a day).
caveats:
SCOPE OF WHAT WAS ACTUALLY VERIFIED. Twelve claims survived the three-lens panel and blind citation audit out of a much larger pool; 140 lower-ranked claims were never verified at all (verification cap of 30), so this report reflects a capped sample of the gathered evidence, not the field. Roughly 30 claims were explicitly REFUTED and are excluded — including, in both directions: the orthostatic circulatory disease harm signal above 2 h/day standing; the head-to-head findings that walking breaks outperform standing breaks on glucose and insulin; the 24-month cardiometabolic and musculoskeletal nulls from two separate trials; the SWAL cardiometabolic and evidence-quality claims; the occupational-standing low-back OR of 1.31; all cost and cost-per-QALY figures; the real-world habitual-use finding that desk owners change posture only twice a day; the 2.6 h/day time-efficiency comparison against walking and stair climbing; and the 31-34% musculoskeletal risk figure. None of those are asserted anywhere above, and their refutation is not softened here — but their removal materially thins both the harm case and the comparator case.

UNANSWERED SUB-QUESTIONS. Of nine coverage areas, eight are only partially answered and one is entirely unanswered. Nothing in the surviving set reports pooled ≥6-month RCT estimates for blood pressure, HbA1c, glucose/insulin, waist, lipids or weight against MCIDs — the discriminator between "standing helps" and "standing is inert" is effectively open. Posture isolation is established only for single lab days; no multi-week step-matched standing-only arm exists at any horizon. All-cause mortality for device-measured standing exists only in one atypical cohort. Cognitive performance and productivity effects were never searched. Costs are a total blank: zero prices, zero per-head fleet costs, zero cost-per-QALY, in any currency or year.

SOURCE-QUALITY LIMITS. Four of the nine findings rest on doi.org resolvers (tier T?), meaning the report's provenance chain went through a resolver rather than a verified publisher landing page — though verifiers independently confirmed each through Crossref, Europe PMC or PMC. The Cochrane page returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch (anti-crawler, not paywall); its content was confirmed through two independent sources keyed to the same DOI. The Gao et al. 2017 null is a SECOND-HAND characterisation inside another paper's limitations section, not the primary source, and its authors have a stated interest in that particular null. The SWAL standing figures are in min/work-hours, not min/day; the paper's whole-day standing effect is smaller (47.2 min at 3 months, 39.0 at 12 months), so anyone reading them as per-day figures overstates the effect by about 1.5x.

POPULATION TRANSFER. The question asks about a workday. The mortality evidence is women of median age 80 in free-living conditions. The best blood-pressure RCT is postmenopausal women receiving sit-to-stand transition coaching, not desk standing. The mechanistic LPL evidence is rats and mice. Only the SWAL trial and the UK Biobank cohort speak to the actual population of interest, and only one of those has a health endpoint.

BUNDLING. Every trial here delivers the desk inside a coaching programme, which is why the SWAL desk-vs-programme contrast (-41.7 min/day) is the only clean estimate of what the hardware itself buys — and even that comes with usage guidance attached.

TIME-SENSITIVITY. Sources span 2003 to 2025; the most recent is the August 2025 Circulation trial. Observational cohort estimates and completed RCT results do not decay with time, so age is not a defect here — but the field is active, and the SWAL 24-month follow-up that would have extended the durability picture was cancelled by covid-19 and does not exist.
openQuestions: Does device-measured standing time predict all-cause mortality in working-age adults after mutual adjustment for stepping and MVPA? This is the single question that would adjudicate the OPACH-vs-UK-Biobank contradiction, and no study in this evidence set answers it.

Can any intervention actually sustain the 2.6 h/day of standing at which the only cardiometabolic association appears, and does benefit materialise at that dose? Every trial here achieves roughly 40% of it, so the entire null result set may be a test of an under-dose.

What are the harms — orthostatic and venous events, leg pain and fatigue, cognitive and productivity decrements — at intermittent 2-4 h/day desk standing doses specifically, as opposed to 6+ h/day near-continuous occupational standing? Every claim that touched this was refuted, and cognitive/productivity outcomes were never searched at all.

What does a sit-stand programme cost per head in 2026 USD, and what is its cost per QALY against the obvious alternatives (walking-break protocols, step targets, structured exercise, ergonomics assessment)? Zero evidence was gathered on any of these, and all cost-effectiveness claims that were gathered were refuted.

coverage.subQuestion: 1. Dose and adherence: device-measured minutes/day of sitting replaced by standing at 3, 6, 12, >=24 months; does it decay below ~30 min/day?
coverage.note: Have scattered device-measured points (58 min/day at 3 mo in a coached RCT; ~30.4 min/day pooled average second-hand from Peachey 2020; 78-84 min/day at 18-24 mo but from only n=10 uncontrolled; 23.5% of baseline retained at 12-24 mo, never converted to minutes; 2 posture changes/day in habitual real-world users) - missing is a pooled meta-analytic dose with CIs at each time point from device-measured arms, the SMArT Work primary activPAL results at 3/6/12 months, and any minutes/day figure at 6 and 12 months from a controlled desk-alone arm.

coverage.subQuestion: 2. Cardiometabolic intermediates at >=6 months: pooled estimates + CIs for BP, HbA1c, glucose/insulin, waist, lipids, weight vs MCIDs
coverage.note: Nothing in the set reports pooled >=6-month RCT estimates for ANY of these markers; the only trial-level cardiometabolic data is a 3-month coached RCT (null on BP and glucoregulation for the sit-less arm; 3.33/2.24 mmHg for the transitions arm, SBP failing its own prespecified alpha), plus cross-sectional compositional BP - HbA1c, lipids, waist and weight are entirely unmeasured in the gathered evidence, so the H1-vs-H2 discriminator is effectively open.

coverage.subQuestion: 3. Posture isolation: does standing-only substitution with ambulation held constant still benefit glycemia/insulin/BP, and how durable?
coverage.note: Acute layer is well covered and mostly negative-to-small (pooled d=-0.31 for glucose, null insulin, null SBP; Henson 2020 pooled null; Gao 2017 null; HFLD-vs-LFHD standing-pattern trial reports no standing-vs-sitting contrast at all) - missing entirely is durability: no multi-week or multi-month step-count-matched or stepping-adjusted standing-only arm, and the one 18-24 month activPAL study explicitly had stepping rise alongside standing, so posture is not isolated at any horizon beyond one lab day.

coverage.subQuestion: 4. Hard endpoints in device-measured cohorts: standing vs incident CVD and all-cause mortality after mutual adjustment for stepping/MVPA
coverage.note: CVD is answered (UK Biobank n=75,897, standing null after mutual adjustment for sitting and walking/running), but all-cause mortality for device-measured standing exists only in one atypical cohort (5,878 women, median age 80, mean 0.9 h/d pure standing) - missing is a working-age device-measured standing-and-mortality analysis with stepping mutually adjusted, which is also what would adjudicate the OPACH-vs-UK-Biobank tension.

coverage.subQuestion: 5. Musculoskeletal outcomes: change in low back and neck/shoulder discomfort at >=3 and >=6 months vs MCID, plus new-onset pain signal
coverage.note: Have a 24-month self-reported null (beta -0.02 intensity, +0.03 prevalence, n=93), acute bout-length dose-response (symptom onset at 71 min, 42 min in pain developers), and qualitative new-onset leg pain/swollen ankles from SMArT Work - missing is any pooled effect size with CI for back and neck/shoulder discomfort at 3 and 6 months on a validated scale benchmarked against an MCID, and the primary source for the 31-34% MSD-risk figure at 2-4 h/day, which is currently only a second-hand citation inside another paper.

coverage.subQuestion: 6. Harms and dose-response inside the 2-4 h/day intermittent window (venous, orthostatic, leg fatigue, cognitive/productivity decrement)
coverage.note: Circulatory harm inside the window is well established (UK Biobank: HR +0.11 per extra 30 min/day above a ~2 h/day inflexion for orthostatic circulatory disease; no association below it) and the near-continuous comparator is bounded (Ontario cohort: mixed sit/stand/walk occupations null at HR 0.97) - completely unsearched are cognitive performance and productivity/work-output decrements, and there is no RCT-level incidence of varicose veins or orthostatic events at desk doses.

coverage.subQuestion: 7. Evidence-quality audit: bundling, self-report exposure, registry prespecification, funding/manufacturer involvement, publication bias
coverage.note: Bundling is documented convincingly (SMArT Work's six components with near-perfect coaching fidelity; the 24-month German RCT's psychologist-led standing course; all three Circulation arms getting 7 coach sessions) and the self-report weakness is named, plus the real-world contrast (72% of habitual users got no OH information) - missing is any registry-vs-publication outcome comparison, any funding or manufacturer-involvement mapping, and any funnel-plot/Egger or GRADE certainty rating for the sit-stand literature.

coverage.subQuestion: 8. Comparator effectiveness for the same behavior-change budget: walking breaks, step targets, structured exercise, ergonomics programs
coverage.note: Acute and cross-sectional comparators are strong (walking breaks beat standing head-to-head on glucose d=-0.30 and insulin d=-0.54; 2.6 h standing needed to match 64 min walking or 5 min stair climbing; 5 min of exercise-like activity gives -0.68 mmHg SBP vs 78 min standing for 1 mmHg DBP) - missing is any >=6-month RCT comparator on the same intermediate markers or hard endpoints, and ergonomics-assessment programs have not been searched at all.

coverage.subQuestion: 9. Actual costs and cost-effectiveness in 2026 USD: converter and desk street prices, employer per-head fleet cost, cost per QALY vs alternatives
coverage.note: Zero evidence gathered - no prices, no per-head fleet cost, no published cost-per-QALY or ROI for sit-stand programs or for the movement-break/exercise-subsidy comparators, so the $150-1,500 individual and $400-900 per-head figures the decision rests on are entirely unverified.

The effect size and CI: Results section — For standing time, compared with the referent 2 h/day, every 30-min increment above 2 h/day was associated with an average HR increase of 0.11 (0.05, 0.18). The abstract repeats it: Standing more than 2 h/day was associated with an 0.11 (0.05, 0.18) higher risk for every additional 30 min/day, and the Methods confirm these are Cox HRs with 95% CIs. 2. The ~11% higher risk gloss is the paper's own wording, not the report author's: Discussion — For standing time, risk increased by an average of 11% with every 30-min increment above 2 h/day. 3. The outcome definition matches exactly: Methods — We defined orthostatic circulatory disease events as orthostatic hypotension, varicose vein, chronic venous insufficiency and venous ulcers. 4. The 2 h/day threshold is the paper's derived inflection/referent point: The reference points were 12 h/day, 10 h/day and 2 h/day for stationary, sitting and standing time, respectively, and For standing time, the risk became more pronounced after 2 h/day for orthostatic circulatory disease. The only part not literally on the page is the closing comparative framing (falls directly inside the 2-4 h/day intermittent standing window rather than only at 6+ h near-continuous occupational exposure). No interpretive leap, no overstated certainty. Note for the report author: the paper is explicitly observational and non-causal (The observational design of our study precludes us from making causal interpretations), and the statement correctly stays in associational language (was associated with).

citationDetail.claim: In this RCT of 127 employees in mostly sedentary occupations, the sit-stand desk intervention's medium-term (6-month) benefits on musculoskeletal complaints and on activation had completely faded by the 24-month follow-up: no reduction in MSC prevalence or intensity and no improvement in vigilance or vitality versus control.
citationDetail.reasoning: Fetch note: WebFetch on the PubMed URL returned only a cookie-consent shell, so I retrieved the same PubMed record through NCBI E-utilities efetch for PMID 36324156 (authoritative record text for that page) and the article's open-access full text via Europe PMC (PMC9632028, linked from the PubMed record). Every element of the statement checks out against the cited article. Design and population: the abstract states a six-month seven-wave randomized controlled trial with employees in mostly sedentary occupations, and the full text gives the exact N: 127 employees in various, mostly sedentary, occupations were randomly assigned to either an intervention or a control group by block randomization (n = 58 intervention, n = 69 control at T0; 98 completed the T24 follow-up). Outcomes named: the abstract enumerates precisely the four outcomes in the statement, musculoskeletal complaints (i.e., intensity and prevalence) and activation (i.e., vigilance and vitality). The core finding: the abstract's no significant intervention effect after 24 months implying a fade-out is stated even more explicitly in the discussion, there was neither a reduction in the prevalence and intensity of MSCs at the 24-month follow-up compared to the baseline nor an improvement of activation in terms of vigilance and vitality. The versus control framing is faithful, since Hypotheses 1 and 2 were both specified as comparisons to the control group. The medium-term (6-month) benefits that the statement says faded are also carried by the article, attributed to the earlier report on the same trial: Konradt et al. [12] found moderate to high inhibiting effects on the intensity and prevalence of MSC after six months of SSD use, and activation improved significantly across six months of SSD use, with the discussion concluding the health effects found on the medium-term level [12] did not persist on the long run. Two caveats, neither large enough to downgrade. First, the statement's completely faded is slightly firmer than the authors' own hedging (effects might fade out over time), though it fairly tracks the unequivocal neither ... nor sentence covering all four outcomes. Second, the article separately reports that early velocity of activation increase predicted long-term improvements in vigilance — but that is a within-person predictor analysis of individual change trajectories, not a group-level intervention effect, so it does not contradict the statement's claim of no vigilance improvement versus control. The one detail not present on the PubMed abstract page itself is the figure 127; I confirmed it verbatim in the same article's full text, so it is accurate rather than embellished. Rated supported: the cited work is exactly the study described, and the load-bearing claim is stated almost word for word.

citationDetail.claim: The measured per-head intervention cost was GBP 228.31 for the sit-stand-desk arm and GBP 80.59 for the identical programme without a desk (2019-2020 pound sterling), so the height-adjustable workstation plus its procurement and installation added roughly GBP 148 per worker — materially below the USD 400-900 per-head figure often cited; the authors also note intervention costs excluded post-trial equipment maintenance.

The two per-head figures (£228.31 for the desk arm, £80.59 for the desk-free arm) are stated exactly; the 2019–2020 pound sterling price year is stated exactly; the cost-component list confirms that the desk arm's distinguishing element is the procurement and installation of height-adjustable workstations; and the limitations text confirms intervention costs excluded post-trial equipment maintenance. The roughly GBP 148 delta is straightforward arithmetic on the two stated figures (228.31 − 80.59 = 147.72) and is fair as an entailment, since the workstation procurement/installation is the component that separates the arms. What the page does not carry is the comparative clause: materially below the USD 400-900 per-head figure often cited. I searched the article specifically for dollar, USD, and $ figures and found no such benchmark, no USD conversion, and no comparison to any other per-head cost estimate. That clause is an external comparison the report is importing from elsewhere while citing this URL, and a reader following the citation would not find it. Everything else is directly supported, so this is not unsupported — but the sentence as written attaches an unsourced benchmark to this source, which is added scope the page does not carry. Hence partial: the numbers, price year, cost composition, and maintenance exclusion are all verified here; the USD 400–900 comparison needs its own citation or should be split out of the sentence.

citationDetail.claim: Versus continued sitting, light-intensity walking breaks reduced postprandial glucose (d = -0.72, 95% CI -1.03 to -0.41) and insulin (d = -0.83, 95% CI -1.18 to -0.48) — effect sizes roughly 2.3x (glucose) larger than standing's, with walking's glucose CI excluding standing's point estimate.
citationDetail.reasoning: Crossref metadata for 10.1007/s40279-022-01649-4 (Buffey et al., Sports Medicine, 2022, The Acute Effects of Interrupting Prolonged Sitting Time in Adults with Standing and Light-Intensity Walking on Biomarkers of Cardiometabolic Health in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis) returns the full structured abstract, which carries every number in the statement. (1) Effect sizes and CIs match exactly: walking vs. continued sitting gave glucose Δ = −0.72, 95% CI −1.03, −0.41 and insulin Δ = −0.83, 95% CI −1.18, −0.48. The statement's label d is correct, not a gloss: the Methods sentence says A meta-analysis was conducted using calculated Cohen's d quantifying the magnitude of difference between experimental conditions, so Δ in the Results is Cohen's d. (2) Comparator direction matches: the abstract explicitly frames these as compared to continued sitting, exactly as the statement says (Versus continued sitting). (3) roughly 2.3x (glucose) larger than standing's is arithmetic on two numbers both printed in the same abstract: standing's glucose effect is Δ = −0.31 (95% CI −0.60, −0.03), and 0.72 / 0.31 = 2.32. The parenthetical correctly scopes the ratio to glucose only, which matters because the abstract reports standing had no significant effect on insulin or SBP — so no insulin ratio is claimed. Hedged with roughly, so no false precision. (4) walking's glucose CI excluding standing's point estimate is verifiable by inspection: standing's point estimate −0.31 lies outside walking's interval [−1.03, −0.41], since −0.31 > −0.41. True as stated. The two derived clauses (the ratio and the CI-exclusion) are simple reads off numbers on the page with no interpretive leap, and neither overstates the source: the paper independently reports a direct head-to-head test in the same direction (walking vs. standing, glucose Δ = −0.30, 95% CI −0.52, −0.08, p < 0.009; insulin Δ = −0.54, 95% CI −0.75, −0.33, p < 0.001) and concludes light-intensity walking was found to represent a superior physical activity break. The statement neither claims the CI-exclusion is a formal significance test nor extends the finding beyond the acute, single-day scope. Source quality is high — Sports Medicine, a top-tier journal, reporting a systematic review and meta-analysis of seven randomised crossover trials. One scope note that does not change the rating: the pooled sample was predominately overweight or participants with obesity in acute 1-day trials, a limitation the statement does not carry, but the statement makes no generalisation claim that this contradicts.

citationDetail.claim: All standing-cardiometabolic associations in this paper are cross-sectional and the authors explicitly state they cannot support causal inference and may be affected by reverse causation, so the 2.6 h/day threshold is not a demonstrated treatment effect.
citationDetail.reasoning: The cited page is the PMC full text of Ahmadi et al., Relationship of device measured physical activity type and posture with cardiometabolic health markers: pooled dose–response associations from the Prospective Physical Activity, Sitting and Sleep Consortium (Diabetologia, 2024). Every clause of the statement is carried by the page's own text. 1. Cross-sectional design for all standing associations: the Methods/abstract state the associations were examined cross-sectionally using generalised linear modelling and cubic splines, and the introduction says the authors conducted a harmonised individual participant data meta-analysis of six cohorts to examine the cross-sectional dose–response associations of device-measured physical activity types (walking, stair climbing, running) and postures (sitting, standing) with cardiometabolic health markers. Standing is one of the postures in that single cross-sectional analysis, so the statement's scope word all is accurate — there is no longitudinal arm in this paper. 2. Explicit authorial disclaimer on causality and reverse causation: the Limitations paragraph reads verbatim, Our observational cross-sectional design limited inferences of causality, and influences of reverse causation may be present. That is the authors stating it themselves, in their own limitations section, naming both causal inference and reverse causation. 3. The 2.6 h/day figure is an associational threshold, not a treatment effect: the Results say a minimum of 2.6 h/day (156 min/day) of standing (z score −0.14 [−0.25, −0.03]) was required to observe more favourable cardiometabolic health, and the Discussion repeats approximately 2.6 h/day of standing was significantly associated with more favourable composite cardiometabolic health. The framing is consistently associated with, and given the limitations sentence above, the statement's conclusion that this is not a demonstrated treatment effect follows with no interpretive leap. The only softening worth noting is wording: the paper says the design limited inferences of causality where the statement says the authors explicitly state they cannot support causal inference. That is a fair, standard reading of a limitations disclaimer rather than an added claim. Note also that the paper separately cites external intervention trials (These results are consistent with intervention trials that reported positive cardiometabolic effects from standing), but those are other people's trials, not this paper's own estimates, so they do not contradict the statement's claim about all standing-cardiometabolic associations in this paper. Rated supported.

citationDetail.claim: Standing that INCLUDES ambulation was more strongly associated with lower mortality than standing without ambulation (Q4 vs Q1 HR = 0.50, 95% CI 0.35-0.71 vs HR = 0.63, 95% CI 0.49-0.81), and its crude mortality gradient was far steeper (50.0 deaths/1000 person-years in Q1 falling to 11.5 in Q4, versus 34.8 to 21.3 for standing alone) — i.e. the stepping-containing posture carried the larger signal.
citationDetail.reasoning: The DOI resolves to Jain P, Bellettiere J, Glass N, LaMonte MJ, Di C, Wild RA, Evenson KR, LaCroix AZ, The Relationship of Accelerometer-Assessed Standing Time With and Without Ambulation and Mortality: The WHI OPACH Study, J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2021;76(1):77-84 (Crossref container-title: The Journals of Gerontology: Series A) — a high-quality peer-reviewed prospective cohort (n=5,878 older women, 691 deaths over 26,649 person-years) in a top-tier gerontology journal. Every numeric claim in the statement is verified against the source, in two independent places. (1) The hazard ratios come straight from the Crossref abstract: all-cause mortality risk was lower among those with more standing without ambulation (quartile [Q] 4 vs Q1 HR = 0.63; 95% CI = 0.49-0.81, p-trend = .003) and more standing with ambulation (Q4 vs Q1 HR = 0.50; 95% CI = 0.35-0.71, p-trend < .001). Both HRs and both CIs in the statement match verbatim, correctly assigned to the right exposure. (2) The crude rates are not in the abstract, so I retrieved the open-access full text (PMC7756713) and confirmed the results table: standing WITH ambulation runs 50.0 / 25.0 / 19.3 / 11.5 deaths per 1,000 person-years across Q1-Q4; standing WITHOUT ambulation runs 34.8 / 25.6 / 22.3 / 21.3. The statement's 50.0 ... falling to 11.5 and 34.8 to 21.3 are exact, and the characterization of the with-ambulation gradient as far steeper is a plain arithmetic reading of those figures (a ~77% drop vs a ~39% drop). The only clause carrying any interpretation is the closing gloss, the stepping-containing posture carried the larger signal. That is a fair descriptive summary of the reported point estimates (0.50 < 0.63; steeper crude gradient) and does not overstate them — the statement says more strongly associated, not that the difference was statistically significant. Worth flagging for the report author, though not enough to downgrade: the paper does not formally test the two HRs against each other, and their confidence intervals overlap substantially, so the comparison is descriptive rather than an inferential finding. The statement's own hedged wording stays inside that boundary. Everything asserted is either stated on the page or entailed by figures printed on it with no interpretive leap.

citationDetail.claim: The dose-risk relationship is non-linear with an inflexion point at approximately 2 h/day of standing (and ~10 h/day sitting): below those thresholds no association with orthostatic circulatory disease risk was observed, so the harm signal begins only above ~2 h/day of standing rather than across the whole range.
citationDetail.reasoning: The cited page is the PMC full text of Device-measured stationary behaviour and cardiovascular and orthostatic circulatory disease incidence (International Journal of Epidemiology, 2024; UK Biobank, n=83,013). Its Discussion states almost verbatim what the statement asserts: the dose-risk association with orthostatic circulatory disease is non-linear, with no association below inflexion points of ~10 h of sitting/day and ~2 h of standing/day. The Results section independently corroborates both halves: the dose-response was non-linear for stationary and sitting time, with risk becoming more pronounced after approximately 12 h/day and 10.5 h/day, respectively and For standing time, the risk became more pronounced after 2 h/day for orthostatic circulatory disease. The statement's closing clause — that the harm signal begins only above ~2 h/day of standing rather than across the whole range — is a direct restatement of risk became more pronounced after 2 h/day combined with no association ... below inflexion points, so no interpretive leap is required. Two minor points that do not change the verdict: the paper gives 10.5 h/day for sitting in Results while the Discussion rounds it to ~10 h/day (the statement's ~10 h/day matches the paper's own rounding), and one Results passage describes sub-referent time as a null to weak protective association rather than strictly null — slightly softer than no association, but the paper's own summary sentence uses no association, which is what the statement mirrors. Note the thresholds are specific to orthostatic circulatory disease, which the statement correctly scopes.

citationDetail.claim: At 24 months the standardized treatment effect on musculoskeletal complaints was statistically indistinguishable from zero in both directions: intensity beta = -0.02 (posterior SD 0.11; 90% CI -0.21 to 0.16; p = .424) and prevalence beta = +0.03 (posterior SD 0.13; 90% CI -0.19 to 0.23; p = .414), i.e. the point estimate for prevalence was nominally in the direction of MORE complaints in the desk group. Analysis N = 93 (47 intervention, 46 control) after 22.9% attrition.
citationDetail.reasoning: The cited PubMed page (PMID 36324156) is the correct article — Konradt et al., Longitudinal Effects of a sit-stand desk intervention - persistence, Fade-Out, and psychological momentum: a Randomized Controlled Trial, BMC Psychology 2022 — and it supports the QUALITATIVE core of the statement: its RESULTS sentence reads Bayesian structural equational modeling revealed no significant intervention effect after 24 months implying a fade-out. That backs statistically indistinguishable from zero at 24 months for musculoskeletal complaints. But the PubMed page is an abstract-only record and carries NONE of the specificity the statement asserts: no beta coefficients, no posterior SDs, no 90% CIs, no p-values, no analysis N, no group split, no attrition percentage, and no observation that the prevalence point estimate leaned toward more complaints. That is exactly the adds specificity the page does not carry case. Note on method: the PubMed HTML returned only a cookie-consent wall via WebFetch, so I retrieved the identical record through NCBI eutils (efetch, db=pubmed, id=36324156), which is the same abstract PubMed serves. I then independently checked whether the numbers exist at all by pulling the open-access full text (PMC9632028) via eutils. Every figure verifies against Table 2 (Coefficients from Latent Residualized Change Regression Models Predicting Health at the 24-Month Follow-up): intensity Intervention beta = -0.02 (PSD 0.11), 90% CI -0.21, 0.16, p = 0.424; prevalence Intervention beta = 0.03 (PSD 0.13), 90% CI -0.19, 0.23, p = 0.414; Note. N = 93; PSD is defined in the table note as Posterior Standard Deviation. Intervention is coded 0 = control, 1 = treatment, so the positive prevalence coefficient does point nominally toward more complaints in the desk group, as the statement says. The methods confirm a final sample of 93 (73.2% of the original sample) of which 47 belonged to intervention group and 46 belonged to the control group, and the results report missing data (22.9% at T24). One small imprecision in the statement even against the full text: 22.9% is the missing-data/non-response rate at T24 (127 baseline to 98 follow-up completers), whereas N = 93 follows three further exclusions, a 26.8% reduction from baseline. Analysis N = 93 after 22.9% attrition merges two different denominators. Verdict: partial rather than unsupported (the cited page states the fade-out finding and is the right article) and rather than supported (the cited page does not contain the statistics; they live in the PMC full text, Table 2). Recommended fix: repoint the citation to https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9632028/ Table 2, or restrict the PubMed citation to the qualitative claim.

citationDetail.claim: Over the actual 12-month trial period (i.e. on observed rather than modelled data), the sit-stand-desk arm was dominated — most costly and least effective of the three arms — while the desk-free coaching programme returned an ICER of GBP 12,091/QALY with only a 42.3-43.5% probability of being cost-effective at GBP 15,000-30,000 per QALY.
citationDetail.reasoning: The cited page is Blackshaw-Blythe et al., The Cost-Effectiveness of the SMART Work & Life Intervention for Reducing Sitting Time (Int J Environ Res Public Health 2022;19(22):14861), PMC9690649. Every element of the statement maps onto explicit text. 1) Over the actual 12-month trial period (i.e. on observed rather than modelled data) — the paper explicitly splits the evaluation into (i) a within-trial analysis considering costs and outcomes estimated over the trial period (12 months); and (ii) a lifetime horizon decision analytic modelling analysis incorporating longer-term... So the within-trial arm of the analysis is exactly the observed-data, 12-month analysis the statement describes. 2) the sit-stand-desk arm was dominated — most costly and least effective of the three arms — the trial randomised offices to one of three arms: SWAL-desk, SWAL-only, or control, where SWAL-desk is SWAL delivered with (SWAL-desk) ... a height-adjustable workstation and SWAL-only without. Results section: The within-trial analysis found SWAL-desk to be dominated by both SWAL only and control (i.e., SWAL-desk being the most costly and the least effective alternative). The abstract repeats it: SWAL-desk was dominated (least effective and most costly). Exact match, including the of the three arms scope (dominated by both other arms). 3) the desk-free coaching programme returned an ICER of GBP 12,091/QALY with only a 42.3-43.5% probability of being cost-effective at GBP 15,000-30,000 per QALY — SWAL-only is the desk-free arm (SWAL without ... a height-adjustable workstation; a champion-facilitated behaviour-change programme, so coaching programme is a fair paraphrase, not an added claim). The paper: SWAL-only was more costly and effective than control with an ICER of £12,091 per QALY; an INHB range of 0.0011–0.0025; and a probability of being cost-effective ranging between 42.3–43.5% (for a £15,000-£30,000 per QALY threshold range). Numbers, range and threshold range all match verbatim. The only interpretive move is the label coaching programme for SWAL-only and sit-stand-desk arm for SWAL-desk, both of which the paper's own definitions license. No added certainty or scope: the paper itself notes cost-effectiveness improved only over the modelled lifetime horizon (SWAL-only ICER £4985; SWAL-desk vs SWAL-only £13,378), which is consistent with the statement's careful restriction to the within-trial result. Rated supported. Note on method: a direct curl of the PMC URL returned a Google reCAPTCHA challenge page (~20KB), so verbatim confirmation was taken from the Europe PMC full-text XML of the same PMC record; WebFetch on the cited URL itself returned the same figures.

citationDetail.claim: In pooled acute crossover trials, replacing prolonged sitting with frequent short standing bouts produced a small but statistically significant reduction in postprandial glucose (Cohen's d = -0.31, 95% CI -0.60 to -0.03) and NO significant effect on postprandial insulin or systolic blood pressure. The upper CI bound (-0.03) is close to null, so the glycemic benefit of posture change alone is small and imprecise.
citationDetail.reasoning: The DOI resolves (via Crossref) to Buffey et al., The Acute Effects of Interrupting Prolonged Sitting Time in Adults with Standing and Light-Intensity Walking on Biomarkers of Cardiometabolic Health in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis, Sports Medicine (2022) — a high-quality, top-tier sports science journal, and exactly the kind of source the claim needs. Every load-bearing element of the statement appears verbatim in the abstract: - Pooled acute crossover trials: the abstract describes A meta-analysis of seven acute, 1-day randomised crossover trials; seven studies were pooled for postprandial glucose, four for insulin, three for SBP. - The effect size and CI: standing as an interruption to prolonged sitting significantly reduced postprandial glucose (∆ = − 0.31, 95% CI − 0.60, − 0.03; z = − 2.15, p < 0.04). The ∆ symbol is the paper's notation for the effect size it defines in Methods: A meta-analysis was conducted using calculated Cohen's d quantifying the magnitude of difference between experimental conditions. So labelling it Cohen's d = -0.31, 95% CI -0.60 to -0.03 is the paper's own metric, not a re-interpretation. - NO significant effect on postprandial insulin or systolic blood pressure: the abstract says standing had no significant effect on insulin or SBP, and separately Both standing and light-intensity walking showed no effect on SBP. - Small but statistically significant: p < 0.04 with d = -0.31 is small by conventional Cohen benchmarks, and the paper itself frames standing as the inferior break, concluding light-intensity walking was found to represent a superior physical activity break. The statement's closing gloss — that the upper CI bound of -0.03 sits close to null, so the benefit of posture change alone is small and imprecise — is arithmetic read directly off the CI the paper reports, not added scope or certainty. It restricts rather than inflates the paper's claim, and is consistent with the paper's own conclusion that walking, not standing, is the superior break. No interpretive leap. One minor note that does not change the rating: the statement says replacing prolonged sitting with frequent short standing bouts, whereas the paper studied *interrupting* prolonged sitting with frequent short standing bouts (breaks within an otherwise-sitting day, not wholesale replacement). The rest of the statement (posture change alone, standing bouts) makes clear the intended meaning is the break condition, so this reads as loose phrasing rather than a misstatement of what was tested.

citationDetail.claim: In the first device-measured (activPAL, 24 h/7 days) observational study of habitual sit-stand workstation use, 18 full-time office workers spent 39% of their daily workstation time sitting and changed desk position on average only twice per day — i.e., real-world users of already-installed sit-stand desks switch posture very rarely.

Verbatim match. 3. 18 full-time office workers — METHODS: Eighteen full-time office workers participated. 4. spent 39% of their daily workstation time sitting — RESULTS: Participants sat for 39% of their daily workstation time. The statement's device-measured framing is slightly generous since the twice-daily position change comes from self-report rather than the activPAL, but the statement attributes the activPAL only to the study's measurement approach, matching the abstract's own phrasing.

citationDetail.claim: In this pooled thigh-worn accelerometry IPD meta-analysis (n=12,095), standing was far less time-efficient than ambulatory activity for the same benefit: 2.6 h/day of standing was needed to match the composite cardiometabolic association of 64 min/day of walking, 5 min/day of stair climbing, or any duration of running.

The equivalence numbers — the abstract Results state favourable composite cardiometabolic health (z score <0) at ~64 min/day walking (-0.14 [-0.25, -0.02]) and 5 min/day stair climbing (-0.14 [-0.24, -0.03]), followed immediately by We observed an equivalent magnitude of association at 2.6 h/day standing. The paper also reports a 13:1 min/day ratio for walking vs stair climbing for the equivalent association, consistent with the same efficiency ordering. 4. The running clause — Any duration of running was associated with better composite cardiometabolic health, and per-minute, every additional minute of running was associated with a z score change of -0.11 (-0.13, -0.09), i.e. roughly 1.3 min of running reaches the same -0.14 z score that takes 2.6 h of standing. So folding running into the list of benchmarks standing compares unfavourably against is faithful to the page, and is reinforced by the paper's explicit claim that standing was least time-efficient of ALL activities. The phrase any duration of running is a mild compression of a per-minute dose-response into the paper's own threshold language, but it does not add scope or certainty the page lacks. The statement is a fair, correctly-numbered summary of the cited article, and the association language (association, not causation) matches the paper's own hedging. Supported.

citationDetail.claim: The minimum standing dose associated with more favourable composite cardiometabolic health was 2.6 h/day (156 min/day), and the magnitude at that dose was a composite z score of only -0.14 (95% CI -0.25, -0.03) - i.e. about one-seventh of a standard deviation, with the CI's lower bound near null.

Calling −0.03 the lower bound is loose terminology (numerically it is the upper bound of the interval; it is the lower bound of the effect magnitude), but it does not misstate any number or the direction, and the substantive claim — that one end of the CI sits close to zero — is exactly what the page's figures show. citationDetail.claim: This is a BUNDLED intervention, not a desk-alone test: every participant received an introductory course in health-oriented sitting (n=100, 78.7%) plus an information flyer, the intervention arm additionally received a dedicated healthy-standing course (n=55) delivered by two trained psychologists with the occupational health service, and only then received the electrically height-adjustable desk. The desk's independent contribution cannot be isolated from the coaching.

The PubMed page itself answered my WebFetch with a cookie-consent wall, so I pulled the record through NCBI E-utilities (efetch, PMID 36324156) and the linked open-access full text through the Europe PMC REST API (PMC9632028/fullTextXML). Both are the same indexed record the cited URL addresses. Every factual particular of the statement is stated verbatim in the article's Methods, in the same sequence the statement describes: (1) all participants received an introductory course in health-oriented sitting; (2) attendance was 100 people, 78.7% (control n = 45, intervention n = 55); (3) 55 intervention-group employees additionally took the healthy-standing course; (4) both courses were led by two trained psychologists in collaboration with the local Corporate Medical Occupational Health Services; (5) each participant then received an information flyer; (6) the intervention group subsequently received an electrically height-adjustable SSD.
