The PubMed record carries only title, authors and a structured abstract (background / methods / results / conclusion) that mentions no course, flyer, psychologist, or participant count. A reader following the cited URL will not find this passage there; they must click through to the free full text. If the report cites page-level detail, the PMC or BMC URL is the more honest pointer. Second, the closing sentence — The desk's independent contribution cannot be isolated from the coaching — is the report author's inference, not a claim the paper makes. The paper's own limitations section lists five limitations (sampling frame, self-report bias, lack of objective desk-usage data, and others) and does not name the bundled-intervention confound among them. That said, the inference is sound and near-entailed by the design as described: the healthy-standing course was delivered only to the intervention arm, alongside the desk, so course and desk are confounded within that arm. Note the sitting course and flyer went to both arms and so are balanced; it is specifically the standing course that travels with the desk. One minor looseness: every participant received an introductory course ... (n=100, 78.7%) pairs two of the paper's own statements that sit slightly awkwardly together — the paper says all participants received the course, then reports that 100 (78.7%) actually attended it. Both numbers are the paper's; the phrasing just blurs offered-versus-attended.

citationDetail.claim: In the UK Biobank accelerometer cohort (75,897 adults for CVD, 6,829 events, mean 6.9 years follow-up), device-measured standing time showed NO association with major CVD incidence (coronary heart disease, heart failure, stroke), while sitting above 10 h/day carried an average HR increase of 0.15 (95% CI 0.11, 0.19) per extra hour and stationary time above 12 h/day an average HR increase of 0.13 (0.10, 0.16) per hour.

Each element of the statement maps to explicit text on the page with no interpretive leap: - Cohort/events: Our CVD incidence sample included 75 897 participants with 6829 events. Matches 75,897 adults for CVD, 6,829 events. - Follow-up: During 6.9 (±0.9) years of follow-up — matches mean 6.9 years follow-up. - Standing null result: Time spent standing was not associated with major CVD risk, reinforced in the discussion (Contrary to sitting time, more time spent standing was not associated with a higher CVD risk) and the Conclusions (Time spent standing was not associated with CVD risk but was associated with higher orthostatic circulatory disease risk). No scope, certainty, or specificity is added beyond what the page carries.

citationDetail.claim: The authors flag a harm signal inside the decision-relevant window: they cite a prior meta-analysis reporting that standing 2-4 h/day may increase risk of musculoskeletal disorders by 31-34%.

citationDetail.claim: In this 3-month RCT of 56 desk workers who ALREADY had sit-stand desks and already had low back pain, the fixed 30:15 arm's reduction in worst LBP was 1.33 points on an 11-point NRS (95% CI -1.79 to -0.86) — which the authors judge clinically meaningful against the IMMPACT/Dworkin threshold — while the average-LBP reduction of 0.83 points is explicitly characterised by the authors as smaller and potentially below clinical meaningfulness.

Crossref (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.apergo.2025.104670) confirms the source: Brakenridge CL, Johnston V, Andrews NE, Gomersall SR, Russell T, Smith MD, Do fixed or personalised sit-stand desk ratios improve lower back pain? A randomised trial, Applied Ergonomics 131:104670 (Feb 2026), Elsevier, CC-BY 4.0 — a peer-reviewed ergonomics journal, so source quality is solid. Fifty-six randomised; primary endpoint explicitly the 3-month follow-up; block randomisation described in Methods 2.2. 2. who ALREADY had sit-stand desks — confirmed twice: eligibility required a sit-stand desk/workstation already at their workplace (used ≥2 days/week), and the Discussion says outright our study participants already had a sit-stand workstation (rather than being provided one). 3. already had low back pain — confirmed: eligibility required average LBP ≥2/10 in the previous month. 4. fixed 30:15 arm — confirmed: fixed ratio (30 min sitting:15 min standing). 5. reduction in worst LBP was 1.33 points on an 11-point NRS (95% CI -1.79 to -0.86) — verbatim match, including the CI, and the scale is explicitly an 11-point NRS (0-10). The Dworkin 2008 citation in the reference list is the IMMPACT recommendations paper, so the IMMPACT attribution is correct and not an inference. 7. the average-LBP reduction of 0.83 points is explicitly characterised by the authors as smaller and potentially below clinical meaningfulness — confirmed: the reductions in average LBP (− 0.83 points) were smaller and potentially less meaningful. citationDetail.claim: Favourable cost-per-QALY figures for sit-stand desks appear only under a lifetime extrapolation, and even there the probability of being cost-effective stays below 53%: SWAL-only vs control GBP 4,985/QALY at 36.4-38.8% probability, and SWAL-desk vs SWAL-only GBP 13,378/QALY at 44.8-52.7% probability, with the authors noting considerable overlap in the credible intervals.

Favourable cost-per-QALY figures for sit-stand desks appear only under a lifetime extrapolation — the Discussion states outright: SWAL-desk only appeared cost-effective using a lifetime horizon (versus control and SWAL-only). Within the trial, The within-trial analysis found SWAL-desk to be dominated by both SWAL only and control (i.e., SWAL-desk being the most costly and the least effective alternative). So for the desk arm specifically, the favourable ratio exists only in the lifetime model. No leap. 2. SWAL-only vs control GBP 4,985/QALY at 36.4-38.8% probability — verbatim in the lifetime paragraph: SWAL-only generated an ICER of £4985 per QALY; an INHB range 0.007–0.008; and a probability of being cost-effective range 36.4–38.8% (for a £15,000–£30,000 per QALY threshold range). Exact match (the report's comma in 4,985 is formatting only). 3. SWAL-desk vs SWAL-only GBP 13,378/QALY at 44.8-52.7% probability — verbatim: SWAL-desk was cost-effective compared to SWAL-only at the threshold values considered (ICER: £13,378 per QALY; INHB range 0.007–0.011; probability of being cost-effective range: 44.8–52.7%). The comparator pairing asserted in the statement is exactly the paper's own pairing. 4. the probability of being cost-effective stays below 53% — the two lifetime ranges top out at 38.8% and 52.7%, both under 53%. Arithmetically entailed, no rounding trick. 5. the authors noting considerable overlap in the credible intervals — verbatim: The considerable overlap in the credible intervals for costs and QALY between alternatives suggests a significant level of uncertainty. One thing I checked for and did not find a problem with: the paper does report a within-trial ICER of £12,091/QALY for SWAL-only vs control (probability 42.3-43.5%), which is itself below the UK £20,000-£30,000 threshold. That could look like a counterexample to only under a lifetime extrapolation, but SWAL-only is the arm WITHOUT the height-adjustable workstation, so it does not bear on the claim as written, which is scoped to sit-stand desks. The statement's scoping is precise rather than overreaching. Every number, percentage range, comparator, and the overlap caveat is present on the page.

citationDetail.claim: Posture transitions and sitting volume are behaviorally dissociable: the sit-to-stand arm added 26 transitions/day (95% CI, 17.71 to 33.64) while total sitting time was statistically unchanged (-10 min/day; 95% CI, -34.6 to 14.9), so the BP benefit in that arm cannot be attributed to reduced sitting volume.
citationDetail.reasoning: Per instructions I did not fetch the doi.org link; I queried https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.124.073385, which returned full metadata plus the complete JATS abstract. Source is Circulation (2025-08-26), Impacts of Reducing Sitting Time or Increasing Sit-to-Stand Transitions on Blood Pressure and Glucose Regulation in Postmenopausal Women: Three-Arm Randomized Controlled Trial (Hartman, LaCroix, Sears, ... Rosenberg; N=407, NCT03473145) — a top-tier cardiology journal, so source quality is high. Every quantitative element of the statement matches the abstract verbatim: the sit-to-stand arm significantly increased STST by 26 STST per day more than the healthy living arm (95% CI, 17.71 to 33.64; P<0.001) and did not differ in change to sitting time (-10 min/day [95% CI, -34.6 to 14.9]; P=0.44). The BP benefit in that same arm is stated (significant decreases in diastolic blood pressure ... -2.24 mm Hg [95% CI, -4.08 to -0.40]; P=0.02 and SBP -3.33 mm Hg). The behaviorally dissociable framing is the paper's own conclusion: This trial demonstrated ... the distinct nature of sitting time and STST — and the mirror-image result in the sit-less arm (58 min/day less sitting, no change in STSTs, and explicitly no significant intervention effects on blood pressure for the sit less arm) reinforces the double dissociation. The only clause not stated word-for-word is the closing inference that the BP benefit in that arm cannot be attributed to reduced sitting volume. That is a direct entailment of what the abstract does state — sitting time in the sit-to-stand arm was statistically unchanged while BP fell, and the arm that did cut sitting by 58 min/day showed no BP effect — so no interpretive leap is required. One minor precision note for the report author: the -10 min/day figure is a between-arm difference in change relative to control, not an absolute within-arm change; statistically unchanged is fair (P=0.44, CI spans zero) but the comparison is vs the healthy living arm.

citationDetail.claim: Workstation sitting time showed no relationship with total daily sitting time in this sample, so time spent sitting (or not sitting) at a sit-stand desk did not translate into a measurable difference in a worker's 24-hour sitting total — consistent with compensatory behaviour outside work hours.
citationDetail.reasoning: The cited PubMed record (PMID 29252918 — Mazzotta et al., Usage of Sit-Stand Workstations and Associations Between Work and Nonwork Sitting Time: An Observational Study, J Occup Environ Med 2018;60(5):e268-e272) directly and almost verbatim supports the statement's core factual claim. The abstract's CONCLUSION reads: there is no relationship between the time spent sitting at the workstation, and total daily sitting time. The statement's first two clauses (no relationship in this sample; workstation sitting did not translate into a measurable difference in the 24-hour sitting total) are a faithful restatement, and the 24-hour framing is accurate since sitting was measured by activPAL 24 h/7 days. What the page does NOT carry is the final clause, consistent with compensatory behaviour outside work hours. The abstract offers no mechanism, never mentions compensation, and reports no work-versus-nonwork association result despite the title promising one — the only association it reports is the opposite-direction finding that workstation STANDING time had a significant moderate correlation with total daily standing time (P = 0.02), which complicates a clean compensation reading. The compensation gloss is the report author's interpretation layered on a null result, not something the page states or entails. Two further caveats on scope: the sample is tiny (n = 18 full-time office workers, 47.9 ± 9.2 years, 61% female) and the design is observational with self-reported desk position and time-at-desk, so no relationship here is a null finding in an underpowered cross-sectional sample rather than a demonstrated absence of effect. The statement's hedge in this sample handles that honestly. Rated partial rather than supported solely because of the unsourced compensatory-behaviour interpretation; the empirical claim itself is solidly on the page. Note on retrieval: the PubMed HTML page returns only a cookie-consent shell to automated fetchers. The record was retrieved from the same NCBI source via eutils efetch (db=pubmed&id=29252918&rettype=abstract), which returns the identical abstract, so the URL is reachable and correct — not unreachable.

citationDetail.claim: For the same time budget, exercise-like activity outperformed standing by roughly an order of magnitude: 5 extra minutes of exercise-like activity was associated with -0.68 mm Hg SBP (95% CI -0.15 to -1.21), and 20-27 minutes of reallocation into exercise reached a clinically meaningful SBP improvement, versus 78 minutes of standing for only 1 mm Hg DBP and no SBP effect at any dose.
citationDetail.reasoning: Fetched the PMC page (ProPASS consortium 24-hour movement-behavior/BP analysis) via WebFetch and independently confirmed against the raw HTML text. Every load-bearing element of the statement appears on the page, essentially verbatim: 1. 5 extra minutes of exercise-like activity ... -0.68 mm Hg SBP (95% CI -0.15 to -1.21) — the abstract states: An additional 5 minutes of exercise-like activity was associated with estimated reductions of -0.68 mm Hg (95% CI, -0.15, -1.21) SBP. The results section separately gives the same figure for replacing 5 minutes of sedentary time. Exact match including the CI. 2. 20-27 minutes of reallocation into exercise reached a clinically meaningful SBP improvement — abstract: Clinically meaningful improvements in SBP and DBP were estimated after 20 to 27 minutes and 10 to 15 minutes of reallocation of time in other behaviors into additional exercise. The results elaborate: a 2 mm Hg SBP improvement from exercise replacing ~20 min fast walking, ~21 min sedentary, ~22 min standing, ~26 min slow walking, ~27 min sleep. 3. 78 minutes of standing for only 1 mm Hg DBP — discussion: substantial replacement of sedentary time with standing or slow walking were required to observe any clinically meaningful change in DBP (78 min/d and 95 min/d, respectively); results: a 1 mm Hg lower DBP was possible through replacing sedentary time with standing ... however, substantial reductions in sedentary time ... were required to observe such a change (eg, 78 minutes ...). 4. no SBP effect at any dose for standing — the same discussion sentence continues ...with no possible reallocation yielding a clinically significant change in SBP, and the results state There was no association between time spent standing, slow walking, or fast walking, relative to other behaviors, and SBP and No reallocation between any amount of time spent standing, slow walking, or fast walking yielded a clinically significant change. The only element not literally printed on the page is the roughly an order of magnitude gloss, which is the report author's arithmetic on the page's own numbers: 0.68 mm Hg per 5 min of exercise = 0.136 mm Hg/min, versus 1 mm Hg per 78 min of standing = 0.0128 mm Hg/min, a ~10.6x ratio. That is a mechanical computation, not an interpretive leap, and it is if anything conservative — on SBP specifically the page reports exercise has an effect and standing has none at any dose. The statement is also careful to keep the units straight (SBP for exercise, DBP for standing), matching how the paper reports them. Rated supported.

citationDetail.claim: In this 78-cluster, 756-participant three-arm RCT, the height-adjustable desk arm reduced device-measured (activPAL) daily sitting by 63.7 min/day vs control at 12 months (95% CI -80.1 to -47.4), and the desk added only 41.7 min/day (95% CI -56.3 to -27.0) on top of the identical behaviour-change programme delivered without a desk (-22.2 min/day, 95% CI -38.8 to -5.7). Every numeric element of the statement matches the page directly: 1. 78-cluster, 756-participant three-arm RCT — the page describes a three-arm cluster RCT of 756 desk-based employees across 78 clusters (SWAL 27 clusters/249 participants; SWAL plus desk 25/240; control 26/267). 2. device-measured (activPAL) — the primary outcome is stated as daily sitting time across all waking hours at 12 months measured with the activPAL3 micro accelerometer. 3. -63.7 min/day vs control at 12 months (95% CI -80.1 to -47.4) — verbatim in the abstract Results. 4. -22.2 min/day, 95% CI -38.8 to -5.7 for the programme without a desk — verbatim in the abstract Results. 5. the desk added only 41.7 min/day (95% CI -56.3 to -27.0) — the page reports SWAL plus desk vs SWAL as -41.7 min/day (-56.3 to -27.0), P<0.001, and characterises the desk arm as threefold more effective. 6. citationDetail.reasoning: The cited URL is the Cochrane review Parry SP, Coenen P, Shrestha N, O'Sullivan PB, Maher CG, Straker LM. Workplace interventions for increasing standing or walking for decreasing musculoskeletal symptoms in sedentary workers. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2019, Issue 11, CD012487.pub2 (published 19 Nov 2019). cochranelibrary.com returns HTTP 403 to automated fetches (both WebFetch and a browser-UA curl returned 403 with a ~5.7KB bot-block body), so I verified the same article's text via NLM E-utilities: Crossref (10.1002/14651858.CD012487.pub2) confirmed title, journal, year and authorship, and PubMed PMID 31742666 / PMCID PMC6953379 returned the publisher's full structured abstract for that exact DOI. That is the same article the URL points at, not a proxy or summary. Every element of the statement is carried explicitly: 1. Search date — SEARCH METHODS: searches were run up to January 2019. 2. Physical-work-environment = sit-stand or treadmill workstations — MAIN RESULTS: Interventions targeted changes to the physical work environment such as provision of sit-stand or treadmill workstations (four studies). 3. The core claim — inside the Physical work environment paragraph of MAIN RESULTS, immediately after the short-term (<6 months) sit-stand results: No studies examined discomfort outcomes at medium (six to less than 12 months) or long term (12 months and more). The parenthetical time-window definitions match the statement's 6 to <12 months and >=12 months exactly, and the sentence's placement scopes it to the physical-work-environment comparison, exactly as the statement scopes it. One caveat worth flagging, though it does not undercut the claim as written: the same paragraph reports that pain-related disability WAS assessed at medium term for sit-stand workstations (No significant reduction in pain-related disability was noted when a sit-stand workstation was used compared to when no intervention was provided in the medium term (MD -0.4, 95% CI -2.70 to 1.90; 1 RCT; low-quality evidence)). The review treats pain-related disability (the impact of symptoms) as a separate outcome from discomfort/symptom intensity, so the statement's gloss zero direct evidence on sit-stand desk musculoskeletal comfort at or beyond 6 months is accurate for comfort/discomfort but would be wrong if stretched to no musculoskeletal outcome of any kind beyond 6 months. As written — restricted to discomfort/comfort — it tracks the source with no interpretive leap.

untraceableStatements: FABRICATED TRIAL COUNT — Summary: "pooled across seven acute crossover trials, standing breaks cut postprandial glucose by only d = -0.31". Claim [6] says only "In pooled acute crossover trials" and gives no k. The number seven is inserted and gives the pooled estimate a precision the pool does not license.

FABRICATED POPULATION — Summary: "belongs to a sit-to-stand *transition* arm in postmenopausal women" and Finding 7: "sit-to-stand *transitions* in postmenopausal women". Claim [3] names no population at all. "Postmenopausal women" appears nowhere in the pool, yet it is doing load-bearing work: it is the report's stated reason for discounting the only randomised BP result.

DROPPED TIMEPOINT — Claim [3] is explicitly "versus control at 3 months". Both the summary and Finding 7 present the -2.24 / -3.33 mmHg result with no timepoint. Checklist item 2 asked for cardiometabolic outcomes at >=6 months; the flagship BP evidence is a 3-month result and the report never says so.

UNSUPPORTED SUPERLATIVES — "the best RCT blood-pressure result" (summary) and "The best randomised blood-pressure evidence" (F7): the pool contains exactly one BP RCT, so "best" is a ranking over a set of one. Same for "In the largest device-measured cohort" (summary/F3) — [7] never claims to be the largest — and "the only dose at which a cardiometabolic association has been observed" (F6).

DROPPED PROVENANCE HEDGE — Summary: "one controlled lab study found continuous standing across a 2-hour OGTT raised lower-body EMG while not reducing glucose at all versus sitting inactive"; F2: "at least one controlled lab protocol found zero glucose benefit despite confirmed muscle activation". Claim [0] carries an explicit warning that this is a rival paper's limitations-section characterisation of Gao et al. 2017, not primary data, and that "the original should be chased". Neither the summary nor F2 retains that caveat. The report is citing a secondhand summary as a primary null and using it as one of only two pieces of posture-isolation evidence.

SIGNIFICANCE-TO-ABSENCE INFLATION — F2: "no measurable effect on insulin or systolic blood pressure". Claim [6] says "NO significant effect". Non-significance is not absence of a measurable effect, and no CIs for insulin/SBP are in the pool, so the precision of those nulls is unknown. Same move in F3: "no association whatsoever with incident major cardiovascular disease" — [7] reports no association but gives no CI for standing, so "whatsoever" asserts a precision the claim does not carry.

CONTRADICTS ITS OWN SOURCE — F1: "the desk (not the coaching) is what delivers it". Claim [8] reports the behaviour-change programme WITHOUT a desk cut sitting by 22.2 min/day with a CI excluding zero (-38.8 to -5.7) — roughly 35% of the 63.7 min total. The coaching demonstrably delivers a significant share; the desk adds 41.7 on top. The parenthetical reverses a finding the claim states plainly.

n=1 GENERALISED — F1: "reliably converts about one hour of daily sitting into standing" and "one hour is the ceiling the best trial achieves". The pool contains one desk RCT ([8]/[9]/[11]). "Reliably" and "ceiling" are claims about a literature; the evidence is a single trial with no replication in the pool.

UNLICENSED INFERENCE (most material) — Summary: "pointing the benefit, if any, at sitting reduction rather than at standing itself"; F4: "The mechanism with the most cohort support is reducing sitting hours... which matters because the desk demonstrably delivers the former (about one hour)". Claim [7]'s hazard gradient exists only ABOVE 10 h/day sitting (and >12 h stationary). Nothing in the pool shows that removing ~1 h/day from an unstated baseline — which for UK office workers is typically well under 10 h — buys anything. The report converts a threshold association into a linear benefit and then hands the desk the credit. This is the single most action-relevant sentence in the report and it is not supported.

UNIT CONFLATION — F6: "Every trial in this evidence set delivers standing well below the only dose at which a cardiometabolic association has been observed". [11] reports a between-arm INCREMENT in standing (+74.4 min at 3 mo, +58.8 at 12 mo); [4]'s 2.6 h/day is an ABSOLUTE daily exposure. Absolute standing time in either trial arm appears nowhere in the pool, so the comparison cannot be made. If baseline standing were ~1.6 h/day the desk arm would sit at the threshold, not "well below" it. (The same increment-vs-total slip is inherited from claim [8]'s own "about one hour, not the 2-4 h/day" framing and was repeated without checking.) "Every trial" also overstates: there is one trial with a standing dose.

MECHANISM INSERTED — F9: "A mechanistic pillar frequently invoked for sitting harm — inactivity-suppressed muscle lipoprotein lipase — rests, in this paper, entirely on rodents". Claim [1] never mentions lipoprotein lipase or any specific mechanism; it says only that the paper is entirely rodent across three muscle types and acute/11-day models. The LPL identification comes from the steelman persona brief, not from evidence. "Frequently invoked" is also unsourced.

HEDGE SOFTENED — Summary: "stepping essentially unchanged". [9]'s 12-month stepping difference is 5.4 min/day with CI 1.8 to 9.0 — statistically significant. Small, but the summary's phrasing implies a null where the source reports a positive difference (the source's own wording is "nearly constant").

DATA-INTEGRITY FLAG DROPPED — Summary asserts "no significant reduction in ... upper back symptom intensity (SMD -0.48)" with no CI. Claim [10] flags that the printed interval is unreadable ("-0.96 to 0.00 as printed '-.096'"). The significance verdict for upper back rests on a number the claim itself says cannot be read off the paper, and the report states it as settled.

SILENT ON THE MISSING TAIL — Summary: "the behaviour is deliverable and durable to 12 months". [11] states the 24-month follow-up was removed because of covid-19, i.e. NO evidence beyond 12 months exists. Checklist item 1 explicitly asked for >=24 months. Neither the summary nor F1 discloses that the durability question past one year is unanswered rather than answered favourably.

Summary: "pooled across seven acute crossover trials" — the count "seven" appears nowhere. Claim [6] says only "In pooled acute crossover trials" with no k. Inserted numeric specificity that makes the meta-analysis sound auditable when its size is unknown to the report.

Summary: "belongs to a sit-to-stand *transition* arm in postmenopausal women" and Finding 7: "sit-to-stand *transitions* in postmenopausal women" — claim [3] names no study population whatsoever. The population is invented, and it is load-bearing: it is the stated reason the BP result is discounted as population-remote.

Summary: "one controlled lab study found continuous standing across a 2-hour OGTT raised lower-body EMG while not reducing glucose at all versus sitting inactive" and Finding 2: "at least one controlled lab protocol found zero glucose benefit despite confirmed muscle activation" — claim [0] explicitly flags this as "the authors' characterization of a cited study, not their own data" and says "the original should be chased." That hedge is dropped in both places, promoting a second-hand description of Gao et al. 2017 to a primary finding in the executive summary.

Summary: "In the largest device-measured cohort (75,897 adults, 6,829 events, 6.9 years)" and Finding 3: "In the largest device-measured cohort" — claim [7] says "the UK Biobank accelerometer cohort" and never says largest. The pool contains no cohort census that could license the superlative.

Finding 3: "standing time shows no association whatsoever with incident major cardiovascular disease" — [7] reports no association; "whatsoever" converts an unquantified null into an assertion of zero. No point estimate or CI for the standing–CVD association appears anywhere in the pool, so the precision of that null is unknown and cannot be characterized.

Finding 2: "no measurable effect on insulin or systolic blood pressure" — [6] says "NO significant effect." No insulin or SBP effect estimates or CIs are in the pool, so non-significance is being reported as absence of effect.

Finding 1: "one hour is the ceiling the best trial achieves" and Summary: "the best RCT blood-pressure result" — the pool contains exactly one desk trial with standing data ([8]/[9]/[11]) and exactly one RCT BP result ([3]). "The ceiling" and "best" assert a cross-trial survey the report never performed.

Finding 1: "the desk (not the coaching) is what delivers it" — [8] shows the behaviour-change programme delivered alone cut sitting by 22.2 min/day with a CI excluding zero (-38.8 to -5.7), roughly a third of the 63.7 min total. The parenthetical is true only for standing time ([11], behaviour-only arm non-significant), not for the sitting reduction the sentence is actually about.

Finding 6: "Every trial in this evidence set delivers standing well below the only dose at which a cardiometabolic association has been observed" — two unlicensed moves. (a) The pool reports only between-arm INCREMENTS in standing (+74.4 / +58.8 min/day vs control), never absolute daily standing time, so it cannot be compared with the 2.6 h/day TOTAL-exposure threshold in [4]; a desk-arm worker with 2 h baseline standing plus an hour would clear it. (b) "the only dose at which a cardiometabolic association has been observed" contradicts [3], where a randomised arm produced DBP and SBP changes at a trial-delivered dose.

Summary: "pointing the benefit, if any, at sitting reduction rather than at standing itself" and Finding 4: "The mechanism with the most cohort support is reducing sitting hours, not accumulating standing hours" — [7]'s gradient exists only ABOVE 10 h/day sitting (and above 12 h/day stationary time). The pool gives no baseline sitting time for the desk trial, so nothing licenses the inference that its 63.7 min/day reduction engages that gradient. Finding 4 also silently discards [2], a device-measured cohort that does associate standing-without-ambulation with lower mortality after MVPA adjustment.

Summary: "and stepping essentially unchanged" — at 12 months stepping rose 5.4 min/day, CI 1.8 to 9.0 ([9]), a statistically significant increase. The magnitude claim is fair but the significance is dropped, and the entire posture-isolation argument the summary leads with rests on that comparison.

Summary/Finding 8 (Cochrane): "upper back symptom intensity (SMD -0.48)" is quoted without its interval, and [10] explicitly flags the interval as ambiguously printed ("-0.96 to 0.00 as printed '-.096'") with an upper bound sitting exactly on the null. The transcription caveat is dropped while the estimate is used.

Summary: "the behaviour is deliverable and durable to 12 months" — [11] states the 24-month follow-up was removed because of covid-19, so 12 months is the outer edge of the evidence by accident. The durability verdict never discloses that no longer-term data exist or why.
coverageGaps: CHECKLIST ITEM 2 (cardiometabolic at >=6 months) RETURNED ESSENTIALLY NOTHING AND THE REPORT DOES NOT SAY SO. The pool contains zero claims on HbA1c, fasting glucose, fasting insulin, waist circumference, lipids or body weight from any sit-stand desk RCT at any duration. The only randomised cardiometabolic number is a 3-month BP result from a transition intervention [3]. The scoper called this "the direct H1-vs-H2 discriminator" — it was never answered, yet the summary reads as if the cardiometabolic case was tested and found wanting. Absence of search is being presented as absence of effect.

THE TRIAL THE REPORT LEANS ON WAS NEVER MINED FOR HEALTH OUTCOMES. Claims [8], [9] and [11] all come from the same 756-participant cluster RCT, and only its behavioural outcomes were extracted. That trial reports cardiometabolic and musculoskeletal secondary outcomes; none were pulled. This is the single highest-yield extraction failure in the pool — it is a step-matched posture substitution (checklist item 3) with 12-month health data sitting unread.

CHECKLIST ITEM 6 (HARMS) RETURNED ZERO CLAIMS. Nothing on varicose veins, venous insufficiency, orthostatic hypotension or circulatory events, foot/leg fatigue, or cognitive/productivity decrement — at any dose. The occupational-health-regulator perspective contributed no evidence to the pool at all. Notably, published device-measured UK Biobank analyses of the same cohort as [7] report an ADVERSE orthostatic circulatory association for standing above ~2 h/day; the pool has the CVD-null half of that literature and not the harm half. No guidance-body document (OSHA, HSE, EU-OSHA, CCOHS) on standing-work caps or rest schedules was retrieved. A reader would reasonably conclude harms were checked and found absent.

CHECKLIST ITEM 9 (COST) RETURNED ZERO CLAIMS AND IS ABSENT FROM EVERY FINDING. No 2026 pricing, no per-head fleet cost, no cost-per-QALY, no ROI evaluation. The scoper committed to verifying specific $150-1,500 and $400-900 figures; none appear. For a question that is fundamentally a purchase decision, the report offers no price side of the ledger and does not flag the omission.

CHECKLIST ITEM 8 (COMPARATORS) RETURNED ZERO CLAIMS. No effect sizes for walking breaks, step-count targets, structured exercise or ergonomics-assessment programmes on the same markers. Yet F4 and F5 steer the reader toward stepping ('standing that includes walking carries a substantially larger signal') with no comparator effect size anywhere in the pool — a recommendation direction with no measured alternative behind it.

CHECKLIST ITEM 7 (EVIDENCE-QUALITY AUDIT) ONLY PARTIALLY DONE. No trial-registry record was retrieved despite the extractor persona promising prespecified-vs-published comparison (the P<0.025 alpha in [3] came from the paper, not a registry). No funding or manufacturer-involvement data. No publication-bias assessment or funnel-plot evidence. So the report cannot say how much weight the null findings can bear either.

CHECKLIST ITEM 4 ONLY HALF ANSWERED. [7] gives CVD but not all-cause mortality from the device-measured working-age cohort; [2]/[5] give mortality only in women of median age 80. No isotemporal or compositional substitution analysis appears anywhere — the scoper explicitly asked 'what happens to CVD and mortality when sitting is replaced by standing versus by stepping', which is the exact analysis that would settle the question, and it was never retrieved. No dose-response curve for standing.

CHECKLIST ITEM 5 ONLY THE SHORT-TERM HALF. [10] covers <6 months only. Nothing at >=6 months, and nothing at all on NEW-onset pain or lower-limb discomfort in previously asymptomatic users — which the scoper flagged as the H4 feed. F8 correctly says 'short term', but the report never states that the longer-term and incident-pain questions came back empty.

THE POOL IS SIX SOURCES DOING NINE SUB-QUESTIONS' WORK. Twelve claims, of which three are one trial and two are one cohort. Two of six perspectives (occupational regulator, field ergonomist) and one more (benefits economist) contributed nothing. Source types never touched: trial registries, guidance/standards documents, procurement or pricing sources, cost-effectiveness models, desk telemetry or longitudinal usage logs, candid long-run user accounts, any non-Anglophone occupational-standing literature (Nordic/Japanese), and any 2024-2026 device-measured analysis. The report's skeptical balance is an artifact of which perspectives returned data, not of the evidence base.

NO FINDING STATES WHAT IS UNKNOWN. Four of nine checklist items returned zero usable claims, and neither the summary nor any of the nine findings contains a 'no evidence was found on X' line. Every finding is phrased as a substantive negative result. That is the structural defect: unsearched territory is indistinguishable from searched-and-null in the output the user sees.

Checklist item 2 — the scoper's own "direct H1-vs-H2 discriminator and half of H1's kill criterion" — returned ZERO claims. No HbA1c, fasting glucose, fasting insulin, lipids, waist circumference or body weight at any follow-up, and the only BP result ([3]) is at 3 months in a different design. Never searched: the cardiometabolic secondary-outcome papers of the very trial the report leans on ([8]/[9]/[11] is a 756-participant 12-month RCT that would have reported biomarkers), and any ≥6-month meta-analysis of sit-stand RCT biomarkers. The report renders a verdict without disclosing its designated discriminator was never retrieved.

Checklist item 6 (harms) returned ZERO claims. Nothing on varicose veins, venous insufficiency, orthostatic hypotension, foot/lower-limb fatigue, or cognitive/productivity decrement at any dose; no occupational standing-work dose-response literature; no guidance-body caps or rest schedules. The report mentions no downside at all, so a reader concludes standing is benefit-poor but risk-free. Never searched: regulatory/occupational-health guidance documents and the standing-occupation cohort literature the "occupational-health regulator" perspective existed to fetch.

Checklist item 8 (comparators) returned ZERO claims. No effect sizes for walking/movement breaks, step-count targets, structured exercise, or ergonomics-assessment programs on the same markers or endpoints. The scoper stated the "money belongs elsewhere" branch is unevaluable without this; it remains unevaluable and the report does not say so, even though [5] hints stepping-containing posture carries the larger mortality signal.

Checklist item 9 (costs) returned ZERO claims. No 2026 converter or electric-desk prices, no per-head fleet cost, no cost-per-QALY or ROI for sit-stand programs or for the competing spends. The $150-1,500 individual and $400-900 per-head figures the decision framing rests on were never verified and are never mentioned.

Checklist item 4's core ask — isotemporal / compositional substitution analyses ("what happens to CVD and mortality when sitting is replaced by standing versus by stepping") — returned ZERO claims. No substitution model, no dose-response curve for standing, and no all-cause mortality result from UK Biobank (only CVD incidence in [7]). The single mortality result [2] comes from a different cohort of women with median age 80, which the report itself calls population-remote.

Checklist item 5's ≥6-month leg and its new-onset-pain question returned ZERO claims. [10] is explicitly "<6 months" and covers symptom INTENSITY only; nothing on incident low-back, neck/shoulder or lower-limb pain in previously asymptomatic users — the exact signal that feeds H4. Finding 8's "in the short term" is honest but the absence of any longer-term or incidence data is never stated.

Checklist item 1 has no 6-month and no ≥24-month timepoint. The pool has 3 and 12 months from a single trial, and [11] records that the 24-month follow-up was deleted for covid. No second long-duration trial was retrieved to corroborate the decay estimate, so the ~21% decay figure rests on one arm of one study.

Checklist item 7's evidence audit is almost entirely unexecuted despite a perspective dedicated to it. No trial-registry record (ClinicalTrials.gov / ISRCTN / ANZCTR) was pulled, so the prespecified-vs-published comparison the "trial number extractor" committed to never happened — the only registry-flavoured fact ([3]'s prespecified alpha) came out of a paper. No funding or manufacturer-involvement data, no publication-bias assessment, no count of trials using self-reported vs device-measured sitting.

The "field ergonomist / user" perspective returned ZERO claims. No desk telemetry, no longitudinal usage logs, no abandonment rates, no workplace case studies, no candid long-run user accounts, no anti-fatigue-mat / monitor-height / typing-accuracy material, and no subgroup evidence on who benefits (existing back pain, obesity, shift work). The durability verdict therefore rests entirely on one trial's activPAL data with no real-world usage counterpoint.

Claim [0] contained an explicit instruction to chase the primary Gao et al. (2017) paper. It was never chased, and the unverified second-hand characterization then became one of two pillars of the executive summary's glycemic argument.

No non-English or non-Western sources anywhere in the pool — notably the Nordic, German and Japanese occupational-ergonomics standards and standing-work cohorts, which are the main body of evidence on the harm side of the dose curve.

No dissenting mechanistic human evidence for H1 was retrieved at all: the sedentary-physiology steelman's only contributions to the pool are a null ([0]) and a rodent-only LPL paper ([1]). Human postprandial insulin/triglyceride crossovers, human LPL data and orthostatic vascular-loading studies are absent, so the report's balance reflects what retrieval returned rather than what the literature contains.
planFlaws: LEADING PREMISE IN SUB-QUESTION 1. 'If the 2-4 h/day exposure the question posits is never achieved, the effect-size question is moot' pre-committed the research to a dose-futility verdict and the report duly delivered it — including inheriting the increment-vs-total unit error uncritically (F6). The original question says 'part of the workday', not 2-4 h/day; the scoper invented the dose the question 'posits' and then tested against it.

BINARY KILL-CRITERIA FRAMING MADE GRADED ANSWERS UNREACHABLE. The checklist repeatedly frames outcomes as 'kills H1', 'kills H3', 'flips the recommendation'. No sub-question asks about heterogeneity or subgroups — who benefits (existing low back pain, obesity, very-high-sitting workers >10 h/day) versus who does not. That is a live and answerable question, and it is precisely where [7]'s hazard gradient actually lives, so the framing routed the research past its own most promising lead.

ASYMMETRIC TREATMENT OF NON-HEALTH OUTCOMES. Item 6 asks about cognitive/productivity DECREMENT; nothing in the plan asks about productivity, alertness or comfort as a possible BENEFIT, or about preference/satisfaction as a legitimate reason to buy. The plan can only find reasons not to buy on that axis.

PERSPECTIVE SET SHARED A DELIVERY FAILURE, NOT JUST A BLIND SPOT. Five of six perspectives are distrust-oriented, but the three most decision-relevant ones (regulator, economist, field ergonomist) put nothing into the claim pool. Nobody appears to have checked that the perspectives actually produced evidence before synthesis proceeded, so the report was written on the two mainstream trial/cohort perspectives alone while carrying the rhetorical posture of a six-perspective audit.

NO SUB-QUESTION ASKED WHETHER THE EXTRACTED TRIAL'S OWN HEALTH OUTCOMES EXISTED. Items 1 and 2 were scoped as separate searches (dose here, cardiometabolic there) rather than 'for each desk RCT with device-measured exposure, pull dose AND health outcomes from the same paper'. That split is why one trial supplied three dose claims and zero outcome claims.

Sub-question 1 set the adherence pass mark at "~30 min/day" when the question posits 2-4 h/day. The extraction then editorialized to that mark ([11]: "stays far above a 30 min/day floor"), and the report inherited a "dose is achieved" reading from a trial delivering roughly a quarter of the posited exposure. Item 1 also declared that if 2-4 h/day is never achieved "the effect-size question is moot" — the research found it is never achieved, yet the report never invokes its own moot-ness rule and never tells the reader that no trial has tested the dose the question asks about.

The kill-criterion architecture had no rule for a discriminator that returns nothing. Item 2 (≥6-month cardiometabolic outcomes) came back empty and the report still issued a verdict, converting absence of retrieval into absence of effect — visible in the language "no measurable effect" and "no association whatsoever." A plan built on pre-committed discriminators needs an explicit "discriminator not retrieved → verdict withheld" clause.

The perspective set is five skeptics and one steelman, and the steelman's yield ([0] a null, [1] a rodent-only paper) argues against its own brief. Nothing in the plan checks whether a perspective actually returned evidence supporting the position it was assigned, so a retrieval failure on the pro-standing side is indistinguishable, in the final report, from a literature that has nothing to offer.

"Better for health" was operationalized as cardiometabolic markers + MSK symptoms + CVD/mortality only. Outcomes where one hour of standing is most plausibly detectable — energy expenditure and weight change, fatigue and alertness, mood, cognitive performance, work engagement — could only enter through item 6's harm framing ("cognitive or productivity decrement"), so a genuine positive in that class had no sub-question to land in and the answer "no cardiometabolic effect but a real comfort/alertness effect" was made structurally unreachable.

The three sub-questions that would flip or price the recommendation (6 harms, 8 comparators, 9 costs) were assigned to the two perspectives whose yield was zero, and the plan has no step that notices a perspective returned nothing before synthesis runs. Synthesis treated the pool as the evidence base rather than as a partially-failed retrieval, which is precisely how the report acquired a settled tone about branches it never examined.

Sub-question 3's posture-isolation test accepted the trial's near-zero stepping difference as sufficient isolation, but [9] measures stepping only DURING WORK HOURS. Compensatory (or reduced) non-work activity is unmeasured anywhere in the pool, so "a near-pure posture substitution" — the premise the executive summary opens with — was accepted rather than tested.

Item 4 asked for standing-vs-stepping mutual adjustment but not for the absolute standing exposure in the cohorts, and item 1 tracked only between-arm increments. Neither sub-question ever requested total daily standing hours, which is why Finding 6 could compare a trial increment against a cross-sectional total-exposure threshold without the plan flagging the unit mismatch.
rationales: Two fabricated specifics (seven acute crossover trials, postmenopausal women) and a dropped timepoint on the only randomised BP result are straightforward traceability failures, but the decisive problems are structural. First, F4 and its summary counterpart convert [7]'s above-10-h/day sitting threshold into a linear benefit and credit the desk with delivering it — the one constructive conclusion in the report, and unsupported by any claim in the pool. Second, four of nine checklist items (>=6-month cardiometabolic, harms, cost, comparators) returned zero claims, and the report contains no sentence anywhere saying so; its confident negatives read as searched-and-null when they are unsearched. A reader would conclude harms were assessed and found absent, which matters because the same UK Biobank device-measured programme that supplied the CVD null also reports an adverse orthostatic circulatory signal for standing that never entered the pool. Third, the trial supplying three of twelve claims was mined for behaviour only and never for its own health outcomes, so the central small, imprecise, or unmeasured verdict rests partly on an extraction gap rather than on evidence.

Two hard fabrications sit in the executive summary — \seven acute crossover trials\ (no k in claim [6]) and \in postmenopausal women\ (no population in claim [3]) — and the second is load-bearing, since it is the stated reason the only randomised BP result is discounted. A third defect is the dropped hedge on claim [0]: the pool warns the Gao OGTT result is the citing authors' characterization of someone else's study and must be chased, and the report promotes it to a primary finding in both the summary and Finding 2. Finding 6 contains a genuine analytic error that inverts its own conclusion: it compares between-arm standing INCREMENTS (+58.8 min/day) against a total-exposure threshold (2.6 h/day) the pool only reports as absolute standing time, and simultaneously asserts that threshold is \the only dose at which a cardiometabolic association has been observed\ while claim [3] records BP changes in a randomised arm. Beyond traceability, four of the nine committed sub-questions returned nothing at all — ≥6-month cardiometabolic outcomes (the scoper's own H1-vs-H2 discriminator), harms, comparator interventions and costs — and the report discloses none of those absences. A reader acting on it comes away believing standing has a small unproven upside and no downside, no alternative worth pricing, and no cost worth checking, when in fact the harm, comparator and cost evidence was never looked at and the biomarker discriminator was never retrieved.

refuted.claim: The paper cites a systematic review (Peachey et al., 2020) finding that lifestyle interventions replacing sitting with standing and/or brief walking breaks reduced sitting time by an average of only 30.4 min/day — at or below the ~30 min/day threshold the dose question flags, and far short of the 2-4 h/day exposure the research question posits. (Second-hand characterization; the Peachey review should be pulled directly for its device-measured subset and time points.)
refuted.why: The -30.37 min/day number is quoted correctly, but it is materially qualified and superseded on three counts. (1) SUPERSEDED — stale search window mislabeled as 2020. Europe PMC record for Peachey et al. (BJSM, DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2017-098968) shows the literature search ran inception through July 26, 2017, first published online 23 Oct 2018; 2020 is only the print issue. The pooled -30.4 therefore structurally CANNOT include the landmark device-measured sit-stand trials published after it, which report 2-3x larger displacement: Edwardson et al., BMJ 2018 (SMArT Work, DOI 10.1136/bmj.k3870), thigh-worn accelerometer, occupational sitting -50.62 min/workday at 3 mo, -64.40 at 6 mo, and -83.28 min/workday, 95% CI -116.57 to -49.98, P=0.001 at 12 months; and Edwardson et al., SMART Work & Life 3-arm cluster RCT (DOI 10.3310/dnyc2141), activPAL3-measured TOTAL daily sitting, desk arm 63.7 minutes per day (97.5% CI -80.0 to -47.4; p < 0.001) less than control at 12 months. So 30.4 min/day is a 2017-vintage average, not the current measured ceiling. (2) WRONG SUBSET — the claim applies an all-intervention pooled average to the specific standing/walking-break case, but Peachey's own environmental (workstation/sit-stand desk) subgroup was -40.59 min/day (95% CI -61.65 to -19.53), while behaviour-only (-23.87) drags the pooled figure down. Peachey also pooled self-report AND device measures, so 30.4 is not a device-measured standing-desk estimate — precisely the caveat the claim itself flags but then argues from anyway. Cochrane (Shrestha et al., CD010912) is larger still for sit-stand desks specifically: -143 min/day at 1 week, -113 min/day (95% CI -143 to -84) at 3 months, -78 min/day total daily sitting (albeit very-low-quality evidence). (3) INVERTED INTERPRETATION — Peachey's own conclusion reads reduced daily sitting time by an average of 30 min/day, which was likely clinically meaningful. The claim recruits the identical number under only / at or below the threshold / far short, i.e. as evidence the dose is too small to matter, which is the opposite of what the cited source concludes. What survives: even the best post-2017 device-measured trials (64-83 min/day) fall short of a 2-4 h/day standing exposure, so that half of the claim stands — but the ~30 min/day ceiling framing does not.

refuted.claim: Head-to-head, light-intensity walking breaks beat standing breaks on both glucose (d = -0.30, 95% CI -0.52 to -0.08) and insulin (d = -0.54, 95% CI -0.75 to -0.33) — i.e. the incremental benefit of walking over standing is roughly as large as the entire benefit of standing over sitting, and standing captures none of the insulin effect.
refuted.why: Provenance is clean — the supporting quote is verbatim from the Buffey et al. 2022 abstract (verified in Europe PMC full text, PMC9325803): When comparing light-intensity walking breaks compared to standing breaks a significant reduction in glucose (∆ = − 0.30, 95% CI − 0.52, − 0.08; z = -2.64, p < 0.009) and insulin (∆ = − 0.54, 95% CI − 0.75, − 0.33; z = -4.98, p < 0.001) was observed. But the quote licenses ONLY the first clause of the claim (walking > standing on glucose and insulin, with those two effect sizes). Everything after the em dash is unsupported by the quote as given. OVERREACH 1 — a number the quote does not state. the incremental benefit of walking over standing is roughly as large as the entire benefit of standing over sitting requires the standing-vs-sitting effect size. The quote contains no standing-vs-sitting figure at all. (The paper reports it in an adjacent, uncited sentence: glucose ∆ = − 0.31, 95% CI − 0.60, − 0.03.) The comparison is arithmetic performed on a number outside the supplied evidence. OVERREACH 2 — the same clause is false for insulin, the outcome it is attached to. The claim asserts the roughly as large equivalence across both glucose and insulin, but for insulin the paper's standing-vs-sitting effect is null, so walking's increment (−0.54) is not roughly as large as the standing benefit — it is the whole effect. The claim's own two halves contradict each other (equivalence, then standing captures none). OVERREACH 3 — dropped hedge / non-significance converted to a categorical zero. standing captures none of the insulin effect appears nowhere in the quote. The paper's actual wording is Standing as a sedentary break showed no significant effect on postprandial insulin compared to prolonged sitting (p < 0.06), and the authors immediately hedge it: only n = 4 studies measured insulin, perhaps with an increased number of studies or larger [samples] the result would differ. A borderline non-significant pooled estimate from four studies is restated as an established null (captures none). MINOR — metric relabel: the quote reports ∆ =, the claim writes d =. The paper's Methods do say Cohen's d underlies the aggregated delta, so this is defensible in the world, but it is a substitution not present in the quoted text. Net: roughly half the claim (the interpretive gloss that carries all its rhetorical force) is not licensed by the cited quote, and one part of it is contradicted by the source paper.

refuted.claim: Reducing device-measured sitting time by 58 min/day for 3 months produced no significant effect on blood pressure and no effect on glucoregulatory outcomes (fasting glucose/insulin measures) in 407 overweight/obese postmenopausal women.
refuted.why: The quote is verbatim (it matches the Circulation abstract exactly), but it does not license the claim as stated. Three specific defects: (1) DROPPED SCOPE CONDITION THE QUOTE ITSELF CARRIES. The quote is explicitly arm-scoped — for the sit less arm and for either arm — signalling a multi-arm trial. The claim strips that, presenting the null as the trial's finding. The full abstract (Hartman et al., Circulation 2025;152(8):492-504, PMID 40709462 / PMC12342652) shows a THREE-arm trial: healthy-living control, reduce sitting time, and increase sit-to-stand transitions. The third arm — the one that actually corresponds to standing up rather than sitting — DID show significant BP improvement: The sit-to-stand arm had significant decreases in diastolic blood pressure compared with the healthy living arm (-2.24 mm Hg [95% CI, -4.08 to -0.40]; P=0.02) and similar decreases in systolic blood pressure (-3.33 mm Hg [95% CI, -6.32 to -0.33]; P=0.03), and the paper's own Conclusions read Increasing STST improved blood pressure in overweight and obese postmenopausal women within 3 months. Used to answer is standing better than sitting, the claim as written reports only the null half of the trial and inverts the source's headline finding. (2) NUMBER MISSTATED RELATIVE TO SOURCE. Reducing device-measured sitting time by 58 min/day converts a between-arm contrast into an absolute dose. The source says: The sit less arm reduced total sitting time by 58 minutes per day MORE THAN the healthy living arm (95% CI, -82.9 to -33.6; P<0.001). The 58 min is a differential vs. control, not the arm's absolute reduction. (3) NUMBERS ABSENT FROM THE QUOTE. The supporting quote contains none of 58 min/day, 3 months, 407, or overweight/obese postmenopausal women; those come from elsewhere in the abstract, so the cited quote alone does not support the claim. Separately, the gloss (fasting glucose/insulin measures) specifies outcomes the quote states only as glucoregulatory outcomes. Defect (1) is the material one: the claim drops the arm-scoping the quote visibly carries, and the omitted arm is the standing-relevant one.

refuted.claim: Standing beyond 2 h/day was associated with an average hazard ratio increase of 0.11 (95% CI 0.05, 0.18) — i.e. ~11% higher risk — for orthostatic circulatory disease (orthostatic hypotension, varicose veins, chronic venous insufficiency, venous ulcers) for every additional 30 min/day, a harm signal that falls directly inside the 2-4 h/day intermittent standing window rather than only at 6+ h near-continuous occupational exposure.
refuted.why: Verbatim check passes on the first half only. The supporting quote is word-for-word present at PMC11481281 under Multivariable adjusted associations for orthostatic circulatory disease, and the paper does define that outcome as orthostatic hypotension, varicose vein, chronic venous insufficiency and venous ulcers. So the HR figure, CI, referent (2 h/day), 30-min increment and outcome label are licensed. The claim fails on its second clause, which the quote does not license and the source page contradicts. (1) SCOPE INVENTED: falls directly inside the 2-4 h/day intermittent standing window rather than only at 6+ h near-continuous occupational exposure. The quote says nothing about intermittency, occupational context, a 2-4 h window, or a 6+ h threshold. On direct fetch, the paper does not differentiate intermittent from continuous standing, does not isolate desk standing, and does not analyze occupational exposure duration — it reports total daily standing time from device (accelerometer) posture inference in UK Biobank. The claim converts an undifferentiated 24-hour total-standing exposure into a statement about a specific behavioral pattern (intermittent standing at a desk) the study never measured, which is precisely the generalization that matters for the research question. (2) NUMBER RESTATED, NOT STATED: the quote reports an average HR increase of 0.11, an additive increment in the hazard ratio per 30 min. The claim glosses this as ~11% higher risk per additional 30 min. The paper does not state an 11% figure, and the additive-HR-per-increment form does not translate cleanly to a per-increment percentage risk increase (it is not compounding, and the average qualifier over a non-linear dose-response curve is dropped). (3) HEDGE DROPPED: the claim calls this a harm signal, while the paper states The observational design of our study precludes us from making causal interpretations. Associated with is retained in the first clause, but the harm framing plus the invented behavioral window pushes past what the cited text supports. Counter-source is the cited page itself (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11481281/): its exposure definition (total device-measured standing time) and its limitations paragraph.

refuted.claim: In this RCT of 127 employees in mostly sedentary occupations, the sit-stand desk intervention's medium-term (6-month) benefits on musculoskeletal complaints and on activation had completely faded by the 24-month follow-up: no reduction in MSC prevalence or intensity and no improvement in vigilance or vitality versus control.
refuted.why: Quote provenance is clean — I pulled the Europe PMC full text (PMC9632028, BMC Psychology, doi 10.1186/s40359-022-00948-9) and the supporting sentence appears verbatim in the Discussion. But the quote does not license the claim as stated; three specific defects: (1) COMPARATOR SWAP. The quote's only comparison is within-subject: there was neither a reduction in the prevalence and intensity of MSCs at the 24-month follow-up COMPARED TO THE BASELINE nor an improvement of activation... The claim converts this to ...versus control. Baseline-to-follow-up change is not a between-group contrast, and nothing in the quoted text mentions a control group. (The paper's Table 2 does report intervention-vs-control coefficients — Vigilance β = −0.10, p = .203; Vitality β = −0.06, p = .324 — so the substance survives, but that is from text the citation does not quote.) (2) HEDGE DROPPED / STRENGTHENED. The quote reads positive SSD intervention effects MIGHT fade out over time; the claim asserts benefits had COMPLETELY faded. Neither completely nor an unhedged assertion is in the quote, and completely is contradicted by the paper's own co-equal finding (abstract: velocity and, partially, acceleration of health improvements at earlier stages predicted medium-term improvements in musculoskeletal complaints and LONG-TERM IMPROVEMENTS IN VIGILANCE). So no improvement in vigilance as an unqualified statement overstates the source. (3) NUMBERS AND DESIGN NOT IN THE QUOTE. RCT, 127 employees, and mostly sedentary occupations appear nowhere in the supporting quote — they come from the Methods (127 employees in various, mostly sedentary, occupations were randomly assigned... by block randomization). They are true of the paper but unsupported by the text offered as support. Note also that the 24-month analyses rest on n = 93 completers (73.2% retention), not 127; attaching 127 to the 24-month null result misstates the analytic sample.

refuted.claim: The measured per-head intervention cost was GBP 228.31 for the sit-stand-desk arm and GBP 80.59 for the identical programme without a desk (2019-2020 pound sterling), so the height-adjustable workstation plus its procurement and installation added roughly GBP 148 per worker — materially below the USD 400-900 per-head figure often cited; the authors also note intervention costs excluded post-trial equipment maintenance.
refuted.why: Provenance is clean — the supporting quote is verbatim abstract text (The average cost of SWAL-desk was £228.31 and SWAL-only £80.59 per office worker.), confirmed in the Europe PMC full-text XML for PMC9690649. But the quote does not license the claim as stated. Three specific overreaches: (1) NUMBER NOT IN THE SOURCE: materially below the USD 400-900 per-head figure often cited. Nothing resembling USD 400-900 appears anywhere in the article — not in the quote, not in the body, not in the discussion of comparator studies. The claim smuggles an uncited external benchmark into a sentence framed as reporting this source, and performs an unstated GBP→USD conversion the paper never makes (£228.31 in 2019-20 is roughly $290; the £148 delta roughly $188). The source supports neither the benchmark nor the materially below comparison. (2) DERIVED NUMBER + UNLICENSED CAUSAL ATTRIBUTION: the height-adjustable workstation plus its procurement and installation added roughly GBP 148 per worker. The paper never states £148, and never attributes the arm difference to the desk line item. Section 2.3 lists FOUR intervention cost components — training workplace champions and general staff (including staff time costs); managers correspondence time; office motivational materials; and the procurement and installation of height-adjustable workstations — and routes the actual breakdown to Supplementary Table S6, which the claim never consults. Subtracting two arm totals only equals the desk cost if the other three components were identical across arms; the claim asserts an identical programme without a desk as its premise, which the quote does not state and the paper does not confirm. (3) DROPPED SCOPE CONDITIONS. The quoted headline figure is, per Section 3.3, the average intervention cost per ITT individual — an intention-to-treat average across all randomised workers regardless of whether a desk was received or used, measured from a public sector perspective (Section 2.1). The claim recasts it as a flat per-head intervention cost and then compares the ITT-averaged delta against what is evidently a per-unit desk price benchmark — a scope mismatch that flatters the comparison. The claim also drops the authors' explicit generalisability hedge: the average cost of delivering SWAL-only or SWAL-desk is subject to several market and contextual factors. Changes in the prices of constituent elements (e.g., desks, materials, training), economies of scale, local office factors ... all may significantly change the average cost of programme delivery, plus the trial's setting and exclusion criteria could have limited the generalisability of our findings. The one clause that IS source-supported is the maintenance caveat, though it is narrowed: the paper says intervention costs did not consider potential costs beyond the trial (e.g., equipment maintenance, training and staff work time) — the claim keeps only equipment maintenance and drops post-trial training and staff work time. Counter-source for the overreach: the same article, PMC9690649 — Section 2.1 (public sector perspective, 2019-20 GBP), Section 2.3 (four-component intervention cost list), Section 3.3 (average intervention cost per ITT individual ... Supplementary Table S6), and Section 4.3/4.4 limitations and delivery-cost caveats. Full text retrieved via https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC9690649/fullTextXML (saved locally at /tmp/claude-1000/-home-<user>-Desktop-Lab/9e11ce5a-30c7-475c-b67a-0bb78a03d4c7/scratchpad/swal.xml).

refuted.claim: The paper reports that Henson et al. (2020), pooling four large postprandial laboratory studies, concluded that neither glucose nor insulin was decreased by standing versus sitting in the postprandial period — a null for the standing-only substitution on the acute glycemic pathway. (Second-hand characterization within a primary paper.)
refuted.why: The second-hand characterization is FAITHFUL to its source, but its editorial gloss — a null for the standing-only substitution on the acute glycemic pathway — is contradicted on the glucose half by a larger, contemporaneous meta-analysis the iScience paper does not cite. VERIFIED PROVENANCE (passes): I retrieved the primary source via NCBI eutils. Henson J, Edwardson CL, Celis-Morales CA, et al., Predictors of the Acute Postprandial Response to Breaking Up Prolonged Sitting, Med Sci Sports Exerc 2020 Jun;52(6):1385-1393, doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000002249, PMID 31895295. Its abstract states verbatim: Data were combined from four similarly designed randomized acute cross-over trials (n = 129) and Postprandial insulin and glucose were reduced when individuals interrupted prolonged sitting with bouts of light physical activity, but not with standing. So the iScience quote is an accurate rendering of Henson 2020, and no retraction or erratum is attached to PMID 31895295. THE REFUTATION — direct contradiction on glucose: Buffey AJ, Herring MP, Langley CK, Donnelly AE, Carson BP, The Acute Effects of Interrupting Prolonged Sitting Time in Adults with Standing and Light-Intensity Walking on Biomarkers of Cardiometabolic Health in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis, Sports Med 2022 Aug;52(8):1765-1787, doi:10.1007/s40279-022-01649-4, PMID 35147898, published online 11 Feb 2022. Pooling SEVEN randomized crossover trials (vs Henson's four) it reports: standing as an interruption to prolonged sitting significantly reduced postprandial glucose (∆ = - 0.31, 95% CI - 0.60, - 0.03; z = - 2.15, p < 0.04) but had no significant effect on insulin or SBP, concluding Frequent short interruptions of standing significantly attenuated postprandial glucose compared to prolonged sitting; however, light-intensity walking was found to represent a superior physical activity break. This is the same design class, the same endpoint window, and the same comparison the claim calls null. It appeared roughly six months BEFORE the iScience paper went online (2022-08-05), so it was available and uncited — the null is not the state of the evidence at time of writing. Net: the INSULIN half of the claim survives (Buffey independently confirms no significant standing effect on insulin); the GLUCOSE half does not generalize. The claim's own phrasing — neither glucose nor insulin was decreased and a null for the standing-only substitution — overstates by half. SECOND, INDEPENDENT QUALIFICATION: Saeidifard F, Medina-Inojosa JR, Supervia M, et al., The Effect of Replacing Sitting With Standing on Cardiovascular Risk Factors: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis, Mayo Clin Proc Innov Qual Outcomes 2020 Dec;4(6):611-626, doi:10.1016/j.mayocpiqo.2020.07.017, PMID 33367205. Nine trials, n=877, mean 3.81-month follow-up, mean +1.33 h/day standing: fasting blood glucose fell significantly (-2.53 mg/dL; 95% CI -4.27 to -0.79) with no significant insulin effect. A different (chronic/fasting) endpoint, so not a head-on rebuttal, but it qualifies the same direction — standing-only substitution is not glycemically inert. SCOPE DEFECT worth flagging for the research question: Henson 2020's standing arm was standing BREAKS of 5 min every 30 min across 6.5 h — roughly 1 h of standing total — not continuous standing at a desk for part of the workday. The iScience gloss standing versus sitting in the postprandial period flattens that dose, and the claim inherits the flattening. Any downstream use of this as standing desks don't help glycemia would be a dose substitution the underlying trial does not license. Ongoing mixedness (context, not the refutation): Price AG et al., Intermittent standing does not acutely improve postprandial metabolism in university students, J Sports Sci 2024;42(24):2517-2526, PMID 39803911, is a further null in a healthy young cohort; conversely Dey KC et al., Eur J Appl Physiol 2026;126(1):579-589, PMID 40764840, found free-living substitution of sitting with standing+walking lowered waking-hours glucose iAUC (-9.2 mmol/L·16h, 95% CI -18.1 to -0.3, p=0.04). The literature is heterogeneous by population and dose — which is itself a reason the flat null framing cannot stand. Note: WebSearch was unavailable (session budget of 200 calls exhausted); all verification above was done against NCBI eutils primary records, which is a stronger source class than search snippets.

refuted.claim: In this 3-month RCT with thigh-worn activPAL measurement, an intensively coached 'sit less' arm achieved only 58 minutes/day more sitting reduction than control (95% CI, -82.9 to -33.6) - far below the 2-4 h/day standing substitution the research question posits, and the same arm produced no change in sit-to-stand transitions (-1/day).
refuted.why: PROVENANCE: CLEAN. The supporting quote is verbatim page text — it matches the Crossref/Europe PMC abstract of Hartman et al., Circulation 2025;152(8):492-504 (PMID 40709462) word for word, including 58 minutes per day more than the healthy living arm (95% CI, -82.9 to -33.6; P<0.001) and did not change STSTs (-1 STST/day [95% CI, -9.4 to 6.5]; P=0.72). The two numeric facts the claim reports are exactly supported, and control is a fair label since the abstract itself writes (1) healthy living (control). OVERREACH 1 (fatal, quote-support): The quote measures TOTAL SITTING TIME, not standing. Nowhere does it say the 58 min/day went into standing rather than stepping, nor does it report a standing-time outcome at all. The claim converts a sitting-time between-arm difference into a standing substitution magnitude and then benchmarks it against a standing dose. That is a construct swap the quoted sentence does not license — the source's own conclusion frames the finding as the distinct nature of sitting time and STST, not as a ceiling on achievable standing. OVERREACH 2 (number not in the quote): the 2-4 h/day standing substitution the research question posits. The research question as given (standing at a desk for part of the workday) posits no 2-4 h/day quantity, and the quote states no such figure. The comparator that makes the word only load-bearing is supplied by the claimant, not by the cited text. OVERREACH 3 (dropped scope conditions): The quote's sentence sits inside a trial restricted to overweight or obese sedentary POSTMENOPAUSAL WOMEN (N=407), in a free-living 24-hour sedentary-behavior intervention with no workplace or desk component. The claim strips both the population and the setting and deploys the number as a general bound on workday desk standing. MINOR AMPLIFICATION: intensively coached appears nowhere in the supporting quote (the source says only 7 individual health coach sessions across 12 weeks, and all three arms received them, including control). The adjective inflates the contrast the claim is drawing. The claim's arithmetic is faithful; its inference is not. It is refuted on quote-support because the decisive comparison (sitting reduction vs. a 2-4 h standing dose) rests on a variable the quote never reports and a number the quote never states.

refuted.claim: Versus continued sitting, light-intensity walking breaks reduced postprandial glucose (d = -0.72, 95% CI -1.03 to -0.41) and insulin (d = -0.83, 95% CI -1.18 to -0.48) — effect sizes roughly 2.3x (glucose) larger than standing's, with walking's glucose CI excluding standing's point estimate.
refuted.why: REFUTED on two independent counter-evidence grounds. The verbatim quote is accurate to Buffey et al. 2022 (Sports Med 52(8):1765-1787, PMID 35147898, PMC9325803), and ∆ is indeed Cohen's d per the Methods. But the claim's derived comparison and its magnitude are both wanting. (1) The source's OWN direct head-to-head contradicts the 2.3x / CI-exclusion framing. Buffey et al. did not leave walking-vs-standing to indirect inference — they meta-analyzed it directly: glucose ∆ = -0.30 (95% CI -0.52, -0.08; z = -2.64, p < 0.009) and insulin ∆ = -0.54 (95% CI -0.75, -0.33). The authors describe the glucose contrast in their own words as a small, statistically significant improvement. The claim instead builds a naive ratio of two separate vs-sitting arms (0.72/0.31 = 2.3) and tests it by noting walking's CI excludes standing's point estimate — an invalid substitute for a difference test, and gratuitous here because the valid direct test exists in the same abstract and returns a SMALL increment (d = -0.30), not a 2.3x advantage. The exact overreach: roughly 2.3x larger than standing's misstates a d = -0.30 measured increment as a 2.3-fold superiority. (2) The magnitudes are superseded by far larger syntheses that put the walking effect at roughly one-third to one-half the quoted size, with Buffey's point estimates falling OUTSIDE their CIs. Obes Rev 2026 (doi 10.1111/obr.70152), 53 studies / 39 meta-analyzed vs Buffey's 7: walking breaks glucose iAUC SMD -0.33 (95% CI -0.48, -0.17) and insulin iAUC SMD -0.44 (-0.62, -0.27) — -0.72 and -0.83 both lie outside those intervals. Eur J Prev Cardiol 2026 (doi 10.1093/eurjpc/zwag079), 144 studies / 2216 participants: glucose SMD -0.22 (-0.27, -0.16), insulin -0.26 (-0.32, -0.19). Metabolites 2026 three-level meta-analysis (doi 10.3390/metabo16080528): glucose g = -0.28 (-0.49, -0.08), insulin g = -0.22 (-0.36, -0.07), GRADE certainty LOW, glucose prediction interval -1.15 to 0.59 (crosses zero), and explicitly Subgroup analyses did not identify any statistically significant moderators — i.e. interruption modality (standing vs walking) was NOT a significant moderator, directly undercutting the claim's core assertion of a large walking-over-standing gap. (3) Aggravating internal defect the claim omits: Buffey's own text flags BOTH quoted estimates as bias-suspect and near-maximally heterogeneous. Walking vs sitting glucose — Begg's Kendall tau = -0.59, p < 0.05 and Egger's intercept = -3.97, SE 1.18, p <= 0.015, suggested possible publication bias; I2 = 94.0% (95% CI 92.2, 95.3), k = 8 effects. Walking vs sitting insulin — Egger's intercept = -8.58, SE 1.43, p <= 0.009, also possible publication bias; I2 = 95.1%, pooled from only 4 studies. Presenting -0.72/-0.83 as a settled measured effect size, without the publication-bias flags or I2 ~ 94-95%, materially overstates the evidence. Not refuted for provenance: the DOI, date, journal, pagination and quotation all check out, and standing's own figures (glucose -0.31, 95% CI -0.60 to -0.03; insulin non-significant at -0.30, -0.60 to 0.01) are as implied.

refuted.claim: The dose-risk relationship is non-linear with an inflexion point at approximately 2 h/day of standing (and ~10 h/day sitting): below those thresholds no association with orthostatic circulatory disease risk was observed, so the harm signal begins only above ~2 h/day of standing rather than across the whole range.
refuted.why: Quote is verbatim (confirmed by grepping the live PMC page: ...non-linear, with no association for lower risk below inflexion points of approximately 10 h of sitting/day and 2 h of standing/day), and both numbers (2 h standing, 10 h sitting) are stated. Two overreaches remain. (1) DIRECTIONAL RE-READ OF THE NULL. The quote says no association for LOWER risk below inflexion points — i.e. below those thresholds, cutting stationary time buys you no risk reduction. The claim converts this into below those thresholds NO ASSOCIATION WITH ORTHOSTATIC CIRCULATORY DISEASE RISK was observed... so the harm signal begins only above ~2 h/day. That flips the null from no benefit from doing less to no harm from doing it, which is a different proposition. The authors' own next sentence fixes their intended meaning as the first reading: This suggests simple messaging to 'sit less' may not be optimal, as that would not lower the risk for those currently accumulating less than 10 h a day. The claim's payload — a safe zone below 2 h of standing — is not licensed by the sentence cited. (It IS licensed by two OTHER sentences on the same page: up to a certain level, neither sitting nor standing are harmful for orthostatic conditions and, in Results, For standing time, the risk became more pronounced after 2 h/day for orthostatic circulatory disease. The claim is citing the wrong sentence for the point it makes.) (2) HEDGE AND SCOPE DROPPED. Our findings also SUGGEST the dose-risk association BETWEEN STATIONARY TIME and orthostatic circulatory disease is non-linear becomes the flat assertion The dose-risk relationship IS non-linear with an inflexion point at approximately 2 h/day. The epistemic hedge (suggest) and the exposure scope (stationary time) are both gone, and harm signal nudges an observational UK Biobank accelerometry association toward causal harm — the same article states the causal claim is not established: If confirmed to be causal in future randomized control trials, our findings would have implications for patient care. Also unlicensed by this quote: rather than across the whole range. The whole-range no-association finding on the page is about CVD and standing (no association for higher or lower CVD risk throughout the range of standing duration), not about the orthostatic outcome the claim attaches it to. Fix is a re-cite plus rewording, not a discard: swap in the Results sentence (risk became more pronounced after 2 h/day) and restore suggest.

refuted.claim: At 24 months the standardized treatment effect on musculoskeletal complaints was statistically indistinguishable from zero in both directions: intensity beta = -0.02 (posterior SD 0.11; 90% CI -0.21 to 0.16; p = .424) and prevalence beta = +0.03 (posterior SD 0.13; 90% CI -0.19 to 0.23; p = .414), i.e. the point estimate for prevalence was nominally in the direction of MORE complaints in the desk group. Analysis N = 93 (47 intervention, 46 control) after 22.9% attrition.
refuted.why: QUOTE-SUPPORT FAILURE: the supporting quote is a bare table-body fragment with every column header and the table caption stripped out. It contains the four numeric strings and nothing else. Four load-bearing elements of the claim appear nowhere in the quote, and two of them are wrong against the source. (1) Numbers stated that the quote does not state. The quote says nothing about sample size or attrition, yet the claim asserts Analysis N = 93 (47 intervention, 46 control) after 22.9% attrition.
