Checking the full text at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9632028/: baseline was 127 (n = 58 intervention group; n = 69 control group), 98 participants completed the follow-up survey (T24), and the final analytic sample was 93 (73.2% of the original sample). So (a) the 47/46 split appears NOWHERE in the paper — randomization was 58/69, an unbalanced allocation, and the claim invents a near-even follow-up split; (b) 22.9% attrition is inconsistent with Analysis N = 93 — 93 of 127 is 73.2%, i.e. 26.8% attrition. The 22.9% figure can only be derived from the 98 who completed before exclusions (1 - 98/127 = 22.8%), so the claim welds an N to an attrition rate that does not produce it. (2) Scope conditions and labels supplied by the claim, not the quote. At 24 months, standardized, posterior SD, 90% CI, and p = are all inferences from headers the quote omits. These happen to check out — Table 2 is captioned Coefficients from Latent Residualized Change Regression Models Predicting Health at the 24-Month Follow-up with headers β (PSD) | 90% CI | p — but the quote as submitted licenses none of them; a reader auditing the citation cannot get from the quote to the claim. (3) Framing drift. Statistically indistinguishable from zero is a frequentist gloss on 90% Bayesian credibility intervals (the paper's own word is credibility), and 90% is a weaker exclusion bar than the 95% a reader assumes from statistically. What DOES survive: the four coefficients are verbatim and correct (-0.02 (0.11), -0.21 to 0.16, .424; 0.03 (0.13), -0.19 to 0.23, .414), the 24-month timepoint is real, and the directional reading of the prevalence point estimate is fair. The claim's statistical core is sound; its sample-description clause is unsourced by the quote and partly contradicted by the paper. Strip the final sentence (Analysis N = 93 (47 intervention, 46 control) after 22.9% attrition) and re-quote with the table caption and headers, and the claim would pass.

refuted.claim: Over the actual 12-month trial period (i.e. on observed rather than modelled data), the sit-stand-desk arm was dominated — most costly and least effective of the three arms — while the desk-free coaching programme returned an ICER of GBP 12,091/QALY with only a 42.3-43.5% probability of being cost-effective at GBP 15,000-30,000 per QALY.
refuted.why: The quoted numbers are verbatim-accurate, but three credible sources materially qualify or contradict the claim as framed. 1) SAME PAPER, SUPERSEDING BASE CASE. Cox et al. 2022 (IJERPH 19:14861, PMC9690649) designed the study in two parts: a within-trial analysis AND a lifetime decision model, because a 12-month horizon cannot capture the mortality benefit that is the entire mechanism of health gain from reduced sitting. Its Table 1 lifetime results reverse the ranking the claim reports: SWAL-desk was cost-effective compared to SWAL-only at the threshold values considered (ICER: GBP 13,378 per QALY; INHB range 0.007-0.011; probability of being cost-effective range: 44.8-52.7%). The paper's own Section 5 Conclusions state the opposite of the claim's implication: both SWAL interventions could be considered a cost-effective strategy from a public perspective. The claim elevates a secondary within-trial slice over the authors' decision-relevant result. 2) THE DOMINATED FINDING IS NOISE, NOT A MEASURED DEFICIT. Table 1 trial-horizon values: control 0.84243 QALYs (95% CrI 0.82221-0.86420) vs SWAL-desk 0.84187 (0.82246-0.86006) — a difference of -0.00056 QALYs on almost fully overlapping intervals. SWAL-desk's INHB CIs straddle zero at every threshold (-0.04, 0.023 / -0.038, 0.024 / -0.036, 0.024), and P(most effective) is 0.286 for SWAL-desk vs 0.272 for control — near a coin flip. Stating flatly that the desk arm was least effective presents a point-estimate ordering with ~29% probability of being the MOST effective arm as a settled result. 3) THE ONLY 42.3-43.5% FRAMING INVERTS THE FINDING. In this three-arm comparison, SWAL-only's 42.3/43.2/43.5% was the HIGHEST probability of cost-effectiveness at every threshold (control 39.8/37.3/33.7%; SWAL-desk 17.9/19.5/22.8%). Sub-50% among three options is the modal, optimal strategy, not a failure; only misrepresents it. 4) EXTERNAL WITHIN-TRIAL COUNTER-SOURCE. Michaud et al. 2022, Scand J Work Environ Health 48:399-409 (PMC9527777, PMID 35333373) — a 12-month, employer-perspective, WITHIN-TRIAL CEA across 24 worksites (N=630) of a multilevel intervention WITH a sit-stand workstation (STAND+) vs without (MOVE+) — found the desk arm cost-effective on observed data: $4656 per QALY gained at 12 months, ICER $1 (95% CI $0.8-1.4) for each additional minute reduction of workplace sitting time, with a 0.013 EQ-5D HRQoL improvement. Cox et al. cite this themselves and concede STAND+ was deemed cost-effective in the US context. So the desk-arm domination is not a replicated within-trial result; the nearest comparable observed-data CEA found the opposite sign. MINOR PROVENANCE NOTE: observed rather than modelled data overstates it — within-trial costs and QALYs were estimated using regression methods with multiply imputed data (20 imputed datasets, Rubin's Rules) and discounted at 3.5%, i.e. adjusted and imputed, not raw observation. The within-trial horizon IS 12 months as claimed (a within-trial analysis considering costs and outcomes estimated over the trial period (12 months)), and every figure quoted matches the source exactly. The refutation is of framing and completeness, not arithmetic.

refuted.claim: In the first device-measured (activPAL, 24 h/7 days) observational study of habitual sit-stand workstation use, 18 full-time office workers spent 39% of their daily workstation time sitting and changed desk position on average only twice per day — i.e., real-world users of already-installed sit-stand desks switch posture very rarely.
refuted.why: Provenance defect: the claim converts a SELF-REPORTED measure into a device-measured one, and the supplied quote hides that. I pulled the full abstract verbatim from NCBI E-utilities (PMID 29252918; Mazzotta MA, Ferrar K, Fraysse F, Lewis LK, McEvoy M. Usage of Sit-Stand Workstations and Associations Between Work and Nonwork Sitting Time: An Observational Study. J Occup Environ Med. 2018 May;60(5):e268-e272). The METHODS sentence the claim omits: Eighteen full-time office workers participated (47.9 ± 9.2 years, 61% female). Sitting time was objectively measured (activPAL, 24 h/7 days), and time at desk, desk position, and perceptions of desk use were self-reported. So the activPAL device measured ONLY sitting time. Desk position and time at desk were self-reported. The claim's framing — In the first device-measured (activPAL, 24 h/7 days) observational study ... [workers] changed desk position on average only twice per day — attaches the device-measurement warrant to the twice-daily posture-change figure, which is the claim's entire load-bearing point (real-world users ... switch posture very rarely). That figure is self-report, not activPAL output. Likewise the 39% figure is a hybrid: an activPAL numerator over a self-reported workstation time denominator, which the claim presents as a clean device-measured percentage. This is exactly the converts a self-report into fact and drops a scope condition the quote carries failure mode. Secondary defects: (1) the supporting quote states changed workstation position twice daily with no dispersion statistic; the claim adds on average, a distributional characterization the source never states (no mean/SD/median is reported for this variable). (2) the first device-measured ... study restates the authors' own novelty assertion in OBJECTIVE (No studies have objectively measured habitual usage of sit-stand workstations) as established fact. What the claim DOES get right, for the record: n=18 full-time office workers, activPAL, 24 h/7 days, and the verbatim RESULTS sentence are all genuinely on the cited page, and the interpretive gloss switch posture very rarely is licensed by the paper's own CONCLUSION (Office workers with sit-stand workstations rarely change desk position). The refutation rests on the measurement-provenance overreach, not on fabrication.

refuted.claim: In this pooled thigh-worn accelerometry IPD meta-analysis (n=12,095), standing was far less time-efficient than ambulatory activity for the same benefit: 2.6 h/day of standing was needed to match the composite cardiometabolic association of 64 min/day of walking, 5 min/day of stair climbing, or any duration of running.
refuted.why: PROVENANCE DEFECT — the supporting quote is not verbatim page text. Two independent fetches of the cited page (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11058050/, Blodgett et al., ProPASS, Eur Heart J 2024) return the paper's actual sentences, and the phrase comparable magnitude does not appear anywhere in the article; nor does the constructed opener Accumulating at least 5 min/day of stair climbing, 64 min/day of walking or any duration of running was associated with.... The page's real wording is: Results — We observed more favourable composite cardiometabolic health (i.e. z score <0) with approximately 64 min/day walking (z score [95% CI] −0.14 [−0.25, −0.02]) and 5 min/day stair climbing (−0.14 [−0.24, −0.03]); and In comparison, a minimum of 2.6 h/day (156 min/day) of standing (z score −0.14 [−0.25, −0.03]) was required to observe more favourable cardiometabolic health. The offered quote is a synthesized paraphrase presented as source text. SUBSTANTIVE OVERREACH beyond even the real text — the running clause. The paper says only Any amount of running was associated with better composite cardiometabolic health; it reports no effect-size equivalence between standing and running. The claim asserts 2.6 h/day standing was needed to match the composite cardiometabolic association of ... any duration of running, converting a minimum-duration threshold statement into a magnitude equivalence the source never makes (it would imply 2.6 h standing ≈ running of arbitrary duration). The walking/stairs half of the comparison (all three at z = −0.14) is supportable; the running half is not. Secondary: for the same benefit imports outcome/causal framing into what the paper explicitly hedges as cross-sectional association (Our observational cross-sectional design limited inferences of causality), and the quote's at least/a minimum of scope wording is dropped. Verified as accurate and not grounds for refutation: n=12,095, thigh-worn accelerometry, one-stage individual participant data meta-analysis — all confirmed on the cited page.

refuted.claim: The minimum standing dose associated with more favourable composite cardiometabolic health was 2.6 h/day (156 min/day), and the magnitude at that dose was a composite z score of only -0.14 (95% CI -0.25, -0.03) - i.e. about one-seventh of a standard deviation, with the CI's lower bound near null.
refuted.why: The two numbers are quoted verbatim and correctly from Ahmadi et al., Diabetologia 2024;67(6):1051-1065 (PMC11058050). But the claim is materially superseded and contradicted on three fronts. (1) SUPERSEDED BY THE SAME AUTHOR, 7 MONTHS LATER, WITH HARD ENDPOINTS. Ahmadi MN, Coenen P, Straker L, Stamatakis E, Device-measured stationary behaviour and cardiovascular and orthostatic circulatory disease incidence, Int J Epidemiol 2024 Oct;53(6):dyae136 (PMID 39412356, PMC11481281, doi:10.1093/ije/dyae136). Same lead author, 83,013 UK Biobank adults, 6.9 y follow-up, 6,829 incident CVD events. Verbatim: Time spent standing was not associated with major CVD risk. And standing is affirmatively harmful past a threshold BELOW the claim's advertised minimum beneficial dose: Standing more than 2 h/day was associated with an 0.11 (0.05, 0.18) higher risk [of orthostatic circulatory disease] for every additional 30 min/day. Its conclusion: increasing standing time as a prescription may not lower major CVD risk and may lead to higher orthostatic circulatory disease risk. So the claim's 2.6 h/day favourable threshold sits 0.6 h ABOVE the dose at which the same author's later cohort finds harm accruing. Citing the surrogate-biomarker paper as the answer to is standing better for health without this successor is a material overreach. (2) CONTRADICTED BY THE RANDOMIZED CAUSAL TEST. RESET-BP: Barone Gibbs B et al., Effects of Sedentary Behavior Reduction on Blood Pressure in Desk Workers, Circulation, 21 Aug 2024, doi:10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.123.068564, NCT03307343. n=271 desk workers, 3 months, sit-stand desk + coaching + prompter. The intervention successfully increased standing by 0.94±0.14 h/d — and produced nothing: between-group resting SBP change -0.22±0.90 mmHg (P=0.808), DBP 0.13±0.61 (P=0.827), similarly null for ambulatory BP and PWV. Worse, increases in work-time standing (r=0.17, P=0.011) were associated with unfavorable increases in carotid-femoral PWV. A ~1 h/day standing increase — the actionable core of the claim — moved no clinical marker in the one design that can test causation. (3) THE SOURCE'S OWN AUTHOR GROUP PUBLICLY REOPENED THE QUESTION. Holtermann A, Coenen P, Ahmadi MN, Stamatakis E, Straker L, Standing in the shadows: is standing a tonic or a toxin for cardiometabolic health?, Br J Sports Med, 22 Oct 2024, doi:10.1136/bjsports-2024-108232 (PMC11503055) — an editorial by the same team, title conceding the direction of effect is unsettled. Secondary defect (noted, not load-bearing): the source defines the composite as the mean of the normally distributed six standardised scores (BMI, waist, triglycerides, HDL, HbA1c, total cholesterol). The SD of a mean of six correlated z-scores is well under 1, so glossing -0.14 as about one-seventh of a standard deviation applies the wrong SD and understates the effect in the paper's own metric. Also, in a CI of (-0.25, -0.03), the bound near null is -0.03, the UPPER bound, not the lower bound as the claim states. And the source itself concedes Our observational cross-sectional design limited inferences of causality — so no measured effect size exists here at all, only an association.

refuted.claim: This is a BUNDLED intervention, not a desk-alone test: every participant received an introductory course in health-oriented sitting (n=100, 78.7%) plus an information flyer, the intervention arm additionally received a dedicated healthy-standing course (n=55) delivered by two trained psychologists with the occupational health service, and only then received the electrically height-adjustable desk. The desk's independent contribution cannot be isolated from the coaching.
refuted.why: Quote-support fails on three specific points. (1) EXACT OVERREACH — every participant received an introductory course in health-oriented sitting (n=100, 78.7%). The quote says the opposite of every: In total, 100 people (78.7%) took part in the healthy sitting course (control: n = 45, intervention: n = 55). 78.7% is by definition not everyone. I confirmed the denominator in the full text (Europe PMC PMC9632028, BMC Psychology 10.1186/s40359-022-00948-9): 127 employees ... were randomly assigned and In total, 127 (n = 58 intervention group; n = 69 control group) participants completed the initial survey (T0). So 27 participants (21.3%) did NOT attend the sitting course. The claim cites the very number that refutes its own universal quantifier. The flyer clause inherits the same defect: the quote scopes it to course attendees (After the course each participant also received a flyer), not to all 127. (2) SAME DEFECT ON THE INTERVENTION ARM — the intervention arm additionally received a dedicated healthy-standing course (n=55). The quote says 55 employees from the intervention group also participated, and the arm contains 58 (per full text). 55/58, not the arm. (3) DETAIL NOT IN THE QUOTE + PROVENANCE — delivered by two trained psychologists with the occupational health service appears nowhere in the supporting quote. It exists in the article (Both courses were led by two trained psychologists in collaboration with the local Corporate Medical Occupational Health Services of the university) but that is an adjacent full-text sentence the claim did not quote. Separately, the cited URL is the PubMed abstract page (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36324156/); the quoted passage is not in that abstract at all — it is Methods text in the open-access full text at europepmc.org/articles/PMC9632028. The quote is verbatim to the article but not to the cited page, so the citation as given does not display its own support. What DOES survive: the bundling sequence (courses → flyer → desk, Employees in the intervention group subsequently received an electrically height-adjustable SSD) and the inference that the desk cannot be separated from the standing course are licensed by the quoted design. The claim's fatal move is inflating partial course uptake into universal receipt while attaching the contradicting percentage.

refuted.claim: The authors flag a harm signal inside the decision-relevant window: they cite a prior meta-analysis reporting that standing 2-4 h/day may increase risk of musculoskeletal disorders by 31-34%.
refuted.why: The claim is refuted by the very paper it rests on. I pulled the PPASS article XML (eutils efetch, db=pmc, id=11058050) and confirmed the sentence's citation is reference [77] = Coenen P, Willenberg L, Parry S. Associations of occupational standing with musculoskeletal symptoms: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med 2018;52(3):176-183 ... 27884862. I then pulled that meta-analysis's abstract (eutils efetch, PMID 27884862). Three specific defects: (1) WRONG EXPOSURE BAND — the central overreach. Coenen 2018 states verbatim: In the meta-analysis, 'substantial' (>4 hours/workday) occupational standing was associated with the occurrence of low-back symptoms (pooled OR (95% CI) 1.31 (1.10 to 1.56)). The exposed category is >4 h/workday. The PPASS sentence reassigns that 31% to standing for 2-4 h/day — a band that sits BELOW the meta-analysis's own threshold. The claim's framing that this is a harm signal inside the decision-relevant window of 2-4 h/day is exactly backwards: the measured signal is above that window. (I could not obtain Coenen's full text — Curtin espace, VU/VUmc Pure, BJSM, fatcat and CORE all failed or 403'd — so I cannot rule out an unreported subgroup; but the headline pooled estimate the 31 unambiguously maps to is definitionally >4 h/workday.) (2) THE 34% HAS NO TRACEABLE POOLED ESTIMATE. Coenen 2018 reports exactly one pooled OR (1.31). For every other region it states: Evidence on lower and upper extremity symptoms was too heterogeneous for meta-analyses. There is no 1.34 pooled result in the reported findings, so the upper bound of the 31-34% range is unsourced within the cited paper. (3) SCOPE INFLATION. The 1.31 is for self-reported low-BACK SYMPTOMS from a base of 45 cross-sectional and only 5 longitudinal studies; PPASS restates it as musculoskeletal disorders generally. Coenen's own authors call the conclusion tentative as only limited evidence was found from high-quality, longitudinal studies with fully adjusted models using objective measures of standing. SUPERSEDING/CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE at the dose actually under discussion: Agarwal 2018 (Ergonomics, PMID 29115188) meta-analyzed sit-stand workstation studies and found low back discomfort DECREASED (SMD -0.230; -0.30 to -0.51 on a 10-point scale) — opposite in direction. The Cochrane review Parry 2019 (PMID 31742666, co-authored by Coenen, Maher and Straker themselves) found no increase in musculoskeletal symptoms from workplace standing interventions at any region or timepoint, with sit-stand workstation point estimates trending toward LESS symptom intensity (low back SMD -0.35, 95% CI -0.80 to 0.10; upper back SMD -0.48, 95% CI -0.96 to 0.00). Honest counterweight: De Carvalho 2020 (Work, PMID 33074206) found standing did not reduce LBP versus sitting either (SMD 0.60, 95% CI -0.68 to 1.87, I-squared 90%) — but that undercuts a standing BENEFIT, it does not rescue a 31-34% harm at 2-4 h/day. No randomized evidence reproduces that harm figure at desk-standing doses.

refuted.claim: In this 3-month RCT of 56 desk workers who ALREADY had sit-stand desks and already had low back pain, the fixed 30:15 arm's reduction in worst LBP was 1.33 points on an 11-point NRS (95% CI -1.79 to -0.86) — which the authors judge clinically meaningful against the IMMPACT/Dworkin threshold — while the average-LBP reduction of 0.83 points is explicitly characterised by the authors as smaller and potentially below clinical meaningfulness.
refuted.why: Three quote-support defects, in descending severity. (1) NUMBER NOT IN THE QUOTE (and not verifiable in any accessible part of the source). The claim states 95% CI -1.79 to -0.86. The supporting quote contains no interval at all — only the point estimate (−1.33 points). The published abstract (Europe PMC / PMID 41124790) likewise reports only reduced worst (-1.33 points/10) and average LBP (-0.83 points/10) with no CIs. ScienceDirect (403) and the Griffith repository copy (403) were unreachable, so the interval could not be located anywhere in the source. A precision-adding statistic that appears in neither the supporting quote nor the abstract is exactly the states a number the quote does not state failure. (2) HEDGE CONVERTED INTO A THRESHOLD CLAIM. The quote's wording is comparative and vague: smaller and potentially less meaningful. The claim upgrades this to explicitly characterised by the authors as smaller and potentially below clinical meaningfulness. Less meaningful is not below clinical meaningfulness, and the word explicitly asserts the authors stated a threshold judgment they did not state in the quoted sentence. (3) SCOPE CONDITIONS AND ARM ATTRIBUTION ASSERTED BEYOND THE QUOTE. The quoted sentence attributes the −1.33 to nobody in particular (the reductions in worst LBP); the claim assigns it specifically to the fixed 30:15 arm. It also imports 56, 3-month, 11-point NRS, and the eligibility condition who ALREADY had sit-stand desks, none of which appear in the quote. I independently confirmed most of these against the abstract — Fifty-six desk-based workers with LBP … randomised to either a fixed ratio (30 min sitting:15 min standing); or a personalised ratio … After 3 months, fixed ratio participants experienced reduced worst (-1.33 points/10) and average LBP (-0.83 points/10) — so the arm attribution, N, duration and scale are true in the world. But the already had sit-stand desks eligibility condition is NOT stated in the abstract either (it says only desk-based workers with LBP), and it is a load-bearing scope condition for the research question, since it determines whether the trial compares standing-vs-sitting at all or only ratio-vs-ratio. Note on what does check out: Dworkin et al., 2008 is indeed the IMMPACT clinical-importance paper, so the IMMPACT/Dworkin threshold gloss is fair, and the quote's line-broken mean-ingful is consistent with verbatim PDF text rather than paraphrase. Verdict under this lens: the quote is genuine and the claim is broadly faithful to the paper, but the quote does not license the 95% CI, does not license below clinical meaningfulness, and does not license the arm attribution or the already had sit-stand desks scope condition. The CI in particular should be cut or re-sourced to a specific table.

refuted.claim: Favourable cost-per-QALY figures for sit-stand desks appear only under a lifetime extrapolation, and even there the probability of being cost-effective stays below 53%: SWAL-only vs control GBP 4,985/QALY at 36.4-38.8% probability, and SWAL-desk vs SWAL-only GBP 13,378/QALY at 44.8-52.7% probability, with the authors noting considerable overlap in the credible intervals.
refuted.why: The supporting quote is verbatim page text and the four numbers (£4985, 36.4–38.8%, £13,378, 44.8–52.7%) and the considerable overlap in the credible intervals attribution all appear in it. But the claim's load-bearing framing is not licensed by that quote, and is contradicted by the same page. (1) Unsupported exclusivity/scope. The claim asserts Favourable cost-per-QALY figures for sit-stand desks appear ONLY under a lifetime extrapolation. The quote contains no horizon word at all — nothing about lifetime, nothing excluding a within-trial result — so the quote cannot license an exclusivity claim. Worse, the same PMC9690649 page reports a favourable within-trial figure for one of the two comparisons the claim itself enumerates: SWAL-only was more costly and effective than control with an ICER of £12,091 per QALY; an INHB range of 0.0011–0.0025; and a probability of being cost-effective ranging between 42.3–43.5%. £12,091 sits below the paper's own £15,000–£30,000 threshold range, i.e. a favourable ICER at the 12-month horizon. So only under a lifetime extrapolation is both absent from the quote and false for the SWAL-only vs control comparison the claim cites. (It holds only for the desk arm, which the paper found dominated by both SWAL only and control within-trial — a distinction the claim collapses.) (2) Mislabelled comparison. The claim files SWAL-only vs control GBP 4,985/QALY under cost-per-QALY figures for sit-stand desks, but SWAL-only is the arm WITHOUT a height-adjustable desk — the page describes SWAL as organisational, environmental (e.g., relocating waste bins, printers), and group/individual... behaviour change strategies, facilitated by workplace champions, with procurement and installation of height-adjustable workstations costed only in the SWAL-desk arm. The quote's own SWAL-desk... compared to SWAL-only phrasing signals the same split. Attributing the £4,985 figure to sit-stand desks reads a desk effect out of the no-desk arm, which matters directly for the standing-desk research question. (3) Dropped scope condition. The quote conditions the probabilities on a threshold: (for a £15,000–£30,000 per QALY threshold range). The claim states the probability of being cost-effective stays below 53% with no threshold attached, converting a threshold-indexed range into a free-standing figure. The claim also silently drops the quote's affirmative finding that SWAL-desk was cost-effective compared to SWAL-only at the threshold values considered, keeping only the uncertainty half. The arithmetic (below 53% for 52.7% and 38.8%) is fine, and the considerable overlap attribution is sound; the refutation rests on defects (1) and (2).

refuted.claim: Posture transitions and sitting volume are behaviorally dissociable: the sit-to-stand arm added 26 transitions/day (95% CI, 17.71 to 33.64) while total sitting time was statistically unchanged (-10 min/day; 95% CI, -34.6 to 14.9), so the BP benefit in that arm cannot be attributed to reduced sitting volume.
refuted.why: Two distinct overreaches beyond what the supporting quote licenses. (1) CAUSAL/MEDIATION CONCLUSION NOT IN THE QUOTE. The claim's operative payload is the final clause: so the BP benefit in that arm cannot be attributed to reduced sitting volume. The quoted sentence contains no blood-pressure result, no mediation or sensitivity analysis, and no attribution language at all — it reports only two behavioral contrasts (STST count and sitting time). The claim (a) presupposes a BP benefit in that arm, a fact the quote never states, and (b) converts a non-significant between-arm behavioral null into an affirmative causal exclusion. The quote's own numbers forbid that step: the CI −34.6 to 14.9 min/day and P=0.44 are compatible with a ~35 min/day sitting reduction, so cannot be attributed to reduced sitting volume is exactly the absence-of-evidence-as-evidence-of-absence move the quote does not support. Did not differ (the quote) ≠ cannot be attributed (the claim). (2) DROPPED COMPARATOR / SCOPE CONDITION. Both numbers in the quote are BETWEEN-ARM contrasts against the healthy living control: increased STST by 26 STST per day MORE THAN THE HEALTHY LIVING ARM (95% CI, 17.71 to 33.64) and did not DIFFER IN CHANGE to sitting time (−10 min/day…). The claim restates them as absolute within-arm facts — added 26 transitions/day and total sitting time was statistically unchanged (−10 min/day). The −10 min/day is a difference-in-change relative to control, not the sit-to-stand arm's own change in sitting time; that arm could have cut sitting substantially in absolute terms while simply not differing from the control. Asserting sitting was statistically unchanged states something the quote does not state, and it is precisely the premise the claim's causal conclusion rests on. The verbatim numbers (26; 17.71–33.64; −10; −34.6 to 14.9) do match the quote, and STST → transitions/day is a fair expansion, so the defect is not fabricated figures — it is the added causal conclusion plus the between-arm→within-arm conversion. I could not independently re-verify the quote against the page (ahajournals.org returned HTTP 403; WebSearch and Tavily budgets exhausted), so verbatim provenance is unconfirmed, but the refutation does not depend on that.

refuted.claim: Workstation sitting time showed no relationship with total daily sitting time in this sample, so time spent sitting (or not sitting) at a sit-stand desk did not translate into a measurable difference in a worker's 24-hour sitting total — consistent with compensatory behaviour outside work hours.
refuted.why: Provenance is clean: the supporting quote is verbatim from the PubMed abstract's CONCLUSION field of Mazzotta et al., Usage of Sit-Stand Workstations and Associations Between Work and Nonwork Sitting Time: An Observational Study, J Occup Environ Med 2018 May;60(5):e268-e272 (PMID 29252918), confirmed via NCBI eutils efetch: Office workers with sit-stand workstations rarely change desk position, and there is no relationship between the time spent sitting at the workstation, and total daily sitting time. Education about the workstations was limited. The first clause of the claim (Workstation sitting time showed no relationship with total daily sitting time in this sample) is licensed. Two other parts are not. (1) UNLICENSED EXTENSION THAT THE SAME SOURCE CONTRADICTS. The claim says time spent sitting (or not sitting) at a sit-stand desk did not translate into a measurable difference in a worker's 24-hour sitting total. The parenthetical (or not sitting) extends the null finding to standing, which the quote never covers and which the paper's own RESULTS section explicitly refutes: Workstation standing time had a significant moderate correlation with total daily standing time (P = 0.02). The source found a significant relationship on the standing side; the claim asserts a null there. That is the exact overreach. (2) ADDED MECHANISM NOT IN THE QUOTE. — consistent with compensatory behaviour outside work hours appears nowhere in the abstract. The quote reports a null correlation and offers no interpretation; the claim attaches a behavioural mechanism (compensation) to it. The hedge consistent with does not rescue it, because the paper's significant positive workstation-standing / total-standing correlation points the opposite way from a compensation story. (3) Secondary: no relationship in a self-reported desk-position measure on n=18 full-time office workers (activPAL for objective sitting, but desk time/position self-reported) is converted into the stronger did not translate into a measurable difference, dropping both the tiny-sample scope and the self-report dependence of the exposure variable. The abstract also carries a published Comment (J Occup Environ Med 2018 Nov;60(11):e625) that the claim does not acknowledge.

refuted.claim: For the same time budget, exercise-like activity outperformed standing by roughly an order of magnitude: 5 extra minutes of exercise-like activity was associated with -0.68 mm Hg SBP (95% CI -0.15 to -1.21), and 20-27 minutes of reallocation into exercise reached a clinically meaningful SBP improvement, versus 78 minutes of standing for only 1 mm Hg DBP and no SBP effect at any dose.
refuted.why: Three quote-support defects, in descending severity. (1) THE HEADLINE RATIO IS THE CLAIM'S OWN ARITHMETIC, NOT THE SOURCE'S. exercise-like activity outperformed standing by roughly an order of magnitude appears nowhere in the paper, and the supporting quote makes no mention of standing at all. Worse, the ratio is not computable for the endpoint the claim leads with (SBP): the page states There was no association between time spent standing, slow walking, or fast walking, relative to other behaviors, and SBP. A null has no magnitude, so an order of magnitude cannot be derived from an SBP comparison. If the ratio is instead derived from DBP, the source's own figures give 78 min (standing) vs 10 to 15 minutes (exercise) for a clinically meaningful DBP change = ~5-8x, not ~10x — and the claim silently swaps in the 20-27 min SBP figure for exercise while pairing it against a DBP figure for standing. The comparison mixes endpoints. (2) no SBP effect at any dose STRENGTHENS THE SOURCE'S HEDGED NULL. Page text is no association between time spent standing... relative to other behaviors, and SBP — an absence of a detected association within a compositional model, relative to other behaviors. The claim converts this into a positive universal (no effect at any dose), which is both a causal upgrade (association → effect) and a dose-range generalization the page does not assert. (3) DROPPED SCOPE CONDITIONS AND PROJECTION-AS-FACT. The source's standing sentence is a 1 mm Hg lower DBP was possible through replacing sedentary time with standing... however, substantial reductions in sedentary time beyond the baseline average composition were required to observe such a change (eg, 78 minutes...). The claim renders this as 78 minutes of standing for only 1 mm Hg DBP, dropping (a) that the comparator is specifically replacing SEDENTARY time, and (b) the explicit caveat that this lies beyond the cohorts' baseline composition. Likewise, the source says clinically meaningful improvements were estimated after 20 to 27 minutes of reallocation — a modeled isotemporal-substitution projection from cross-sectional ProPASS data — which the claim states as achieved fact (20-27 minutes of reallocation into exercise REACHED a clinically meaningful SBP improvement), and the verb outperformed imports a causal-comparative framing the paper's own wording (was associated with estimated reductions) deliberately avoids. The verbatim numbers the claim does cite (-0.68 mm Hg; 95% CI -0.15, -1.21; 20-27 min) check out against the page exactly. The refutation is that the load-bearing comparative framing — the order of magnitude, the mixed-endpoint pairing, and the hardened null — is not licensed by the cited text.

refuted.claim: Despite ~59-74 min/day more standing sustained for 12 months with ambulation nearly unchanged, the trial found no noticeable between-group differences in any cardiometabolic marker (weight, waist, BMI, body fat, systolic and diastolic BP, HbA1c, total/HDL/LDL cholesterol, triglycerides, fasting glucose, composite risk score) or fatigue at 3 or 12 months; the only physical-health signal was a small favourable change in lower-extremity pain and prevalence in the desk arm at 12 months. Reported table values give a desk-vs-control 12-month systolic BP difference of about 0.6 mmHg (-2.08 vs -1.44) and HbA1c about -0.6 mmol/mol (~0.05%), both well below common MCIDs.
refuted.why: QUOTE-SUPPORT DEFECTS (4). The supporting quote IS verbatim page text (confirmed against https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9382450/, Physical health results paragraph), and the null-cardiometabolic half of the claim is licensed by it. But the claim's exposure clause is not. 1. STATES A NUMBER THE SOURCE DOES NOT STATE (decisive). Claim: ~59-74 min/day more standing. The paper's standing results are: between-group adjusted difference, SWAL+desk vs control, +47.2 min/day (95% CI 34.3 to 60.2) at 3 months and +39.0 min/day (26.8 to 51.3) at 12 months; within-group change +51.1 min (3mo), +32.8 min (12mo). No standing figure in the 59-74 range appears anywhere. The 59-74 range is the SITTING-reduction result being relabelled as standing: sitting fell -62.7 min/day (CI -77.6 to -47.8) at 3 months and -63.7 (CI -80.1 to -47.4) at 12 months, and -68.5/-53.7 within-group. The claim swaps the primary outcome (sitting reduction) for a secondary one (standing gain) and inflates the true standing effect by ~50%. Counter-source: the same article's sitting/standing results tables. 2. DROPS A SCOPE CONDITION THE SOURCE CARRIES. Claim: standing gain sustained for 12 months. The source shows marked attenuation: within-group standing +51.1 min at 3 months decaying to +32.8 min at 12 months (between-group 47.2 -> 39.0); sitting reduction likewise decayed (-68.5 -> -53.7). Sustained erases a documented decay the tables report. 3. INTERVENTION GENERALIZED BEYOND THE TRIAL. The claim frames this as an effect of standing at a desk. The cited arm is SWAL plus desk -- a multicomponent behaviour-change programme (organisational strategies, senior leader support, workplace champions, education sessions) bundled WITH a height-adjustable desk, in a three-arm cluster RCT against usual practice. The desk is not separable from the programme in this contrast; the SWAL-only arm existed precisely because the desk is one component. 4. INTRODUCES A BENCHMARK ABSENT FROM THE SOURCE. both well below common MCIDs -- the article contains no mention of MCID or minimal clinically important difference. That is the claimant's own evaluative standard presented alongside cited table values. WHAT DOES CHECK OUT: the derived contrasts are arithmetically correct off Table 7 and are honestly flagged as derivations (reported table values give): SBP change -2.08 (desk) vs -1.44 (control) = 0.64 mmHg; HbA1c change +1.84 vs +2.42 = -0.58 mmol/mol. Note both arms' HbA1c ROSE; the claim's -0.6 mmol/mol is a between-group delta, not an improvement. The lower-extremity musculoskeletal sentence is a faithful, hedge-preserving paraphrase (small favourable changes... appeared to be). Refuted on defect 1 alone: the quantitative exposure the claim is built on is stated nowhere in the cited source and contradicts the figures the source does report.

refuted.claim: Evidence-quality limit: only the activPAL sitting, prolonged sitting, standing and stepping outcomes were formally tested with P values and confidence intervals; every cardiometabolic, musculoskeletal, psychological and work-related secondary outcome was reported descriptively with no statistical testing and no confidence intervals, and no multiple-testing correction was applied anywhere. The 'small favourable' pain and wellbeing findings therefore carry no inferential support. Funding was NIHR (public), but an author is a co-inventor of the activPAL monitor and a director of PAL Technologies.
refuted.why: The supporting quote is verbatim and licenses most of the claim, but not the universal quantifier no multiple-testing correction was applied anywhere. SUPPORTED elements (verified verbatim in the page text): - Formally tested outcomes: we analysed key secondary activPAL assessed outcomes...: sitting time (at three months), prolonged sitting time, standing time, and stepping time... P values and 95% confidence intervals are presented for these variables only. - Descriptive-only secondaries: For all other secondary outcomes, only descriptive analyses with no statistical testing were performed at three and 12 months: continuous data... summarised as means and standard deviations, and skewed data with medians and interquartile ranges. Cardiometabolic (lipids, glucose, BP, clustered risk score), musculoskeletal, psychological and work-related measures are all in that all other bucket — confirmed present in the Outcomes section. - Funding/COI: This project is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) public health research programme (project No PR-R5-0213-25004) and MHG is a co-inventor of the activPAL3 physical activity monitor and a director of PAL Technologies. EXACT OVERREACH — dropped scope condition, universalized: The quoted sentence carries its own scope limiter, and P values and 95% confidence intervals are presented for THESE VARIABLES ONLY, and it sits inside the paragraph about key secondary activPAL outcomes. The claim strips that scope and asserts the correction failure held anywhere. The same page contradicts the universal in the very next paragraph: Estimates are presented with 95% confidence intervals, with the exception of the primary analysis of the primary outcome (daily sitting time), which are presented with 97.5% confidence intervals. A 97.5% CI on the primary outcome is precisely a multiplicity adjustment (alpha 0.05 split across the two intervention-vs-control comparisons), and the Sample size paragraph names the reason outright: the power calculation used a two tailed significance level of 5%... allowing for multiple comparisons with the control group. So a multiplicity adjustment WAS applied — to the primary comparison — and the claim's anywhere states something the quote does not state and the source refutes. SECONDARY PROVENANCE DEFECT: the claim scare-quotes small favourable as the paper's characterization of the pain and wellbeing findings. The paper's phrase for those outcomes is Small but non-clinically meaningful improvements were found in stress, wellbeing, vigour, and pain in the lower extremity; its actual phrase small favourable changes is used for Axivity-measured steps and light physical activity, not for pain or wellbeing. The quotation marks attribute wording to the source that the source does not use for those outcomes. Fix that would pass: scope the sentence to no multiple-testing correction was applied across the key secondary activPAL comparisons, which were reported with unadjusted P values and 95% CIs (the primary outcome used 97.5% CIs to allow for the two intervention-versus-control comparisons), and drop the quotation marks around small favourable.

refuted.claim: Head-to-head on the same outcome (workplace sitting minutes), the comparator interventions are weak or null: walking strategies produced no significant effect at short term (MD -15 min/day, 95% CI -50 to 19, one study) or medium term (MD -17 min/day, 95% CI -61 to 28, one study), while short breaks of 1-2 minutes every half hour beat two 15-minute breaks by 40 min/day (95% CI -66 to -15, one study, low-quality evidence) — roughly 40% of the desk's short-term effect from a zero-hardware intervention.
refuted.why: The two numeric halves check out verbatim — I refetched PMC6517221 and the supporting quote is verbatim page text (walking: MD −15 minutes per day, 95% CI −50 to 19, low‐quality evidence, one study short-term and MD −17 minutes/day, 95% CI −61 to 28 medium-term; short breaks: reduced time spent sitting at work on average by 40 minutes per day (95% CI −66 to −15)... compared to long breaks (two 15‐minute breaks per workday)). The refutation is confined to the framing clauses the quote does not license: 1) UNSTATED NUMBER / OUT-OF-QUOTE RATIO. roughly 40% of the desk's short-term effect is a ratio the quote never states, and the denominator (the sit-stand desk's −100 min/day) appears nowhere in the supporting quote. The arithmetic only works by importing a separate sentence from elsewhere on the page (reduced sitting time at work on average by 100 minutes per workday at short‐term follow‐up, ⊕⊕⊝⊝ LOW). 2) DROPPED SCOPE CONDITION — the load-bearing one. The 40 min/day is an increment over an ACTIVE comparator (two 15-minute breaks/day, itself a break intervention), whereas the desk's 100 min/day is measured against a plain sit-desk control. The claim states the comparator mid-sentence, then discards it in the concluding clause: roughly 40% of the desk's short-term effect from a zero-hardware intervention reads as an absolute effect size for short breaks versus doing nothing. The quote supports no such absolute magnitude for short breaks. 3) HEAD-TO-HEAD IS FALSE TO THE DESIGN. The review ran no head-to-head trial of these against sit-stand desks: walking strategies were compared vs no intervention, short breaks vs long breaks, desks vs sit-desk. Each is a separate single-study comparison with a different control. Head-to-head... the comparator interventions presents an unadjusted indirect cross-comparison as a direct one, which the quoted text does not authorize. 4) Minor hedge drop: the quote labels the short-term walking result low-quality evidence; the claim keeps that label for short breaks but omits it for walking.

refuted.claim: In this meta-analysis the harm threshold for low-back symptoms was set at MORE than 4 hours/workday of occupational standing ('substantial'), which yielded a pooled OR of 1.31 (95% CI 1.10 to 1.56) — i.e. the pooled harm estimate applies to exposure at or above the top of the 2-4 h/day intermittent window, not within it.
refuted.why: The quote supports only the first half of the claim. Verbatim it says: In the meta-analysis, 'substantial' (>4 hours/workday) occupational standing was associated with the occurrence of low-back symptoms (pooled OR (95% CI) 1.31 (1.10 to 1.56)). That licenses: category label substantial = >4 h/workday, outcome = low-back symptoms, pooled OR 1.31 (1.10-1.56). Everything after the em-dash is unlicensed, and there are four distinct defects. (1) IMPORTED SCOPE THE QUOTE DOES NOT CARRY. The clause applies to exposure at or above the top of the 2-4 h/day intermittent window, not within it invokes a 2-4 h/day intermittent window that appears nowhere in the quote. The quote states one exposure category and says nothing about intermittent standing, sit-stand alternation, or any 2-4 h band. That window is welded on from a different paper (see counterSource) and then framed as if this meta-analysis positioned its estimate relative to it. (2) A NEGATIVE THE QUOTE DOES NOT STATE. not within it asserts that the pooled estimate does NOT apply below 4 h/day. The quote reports no sub-4 h category and no null result for one. Absence of a quoted lower-exposure figure is not a stated finding of no association — this converts silence into an affirmative boundary claim. (3) BOUNDARY MISSTATEMENT THAT CONTRADICTS THE QUOTE'S OWN OPERATIONALIZATION. >4 hours/workday is strictly greater than 4 h and therefore EXCLUDES exactly 4 h. The claim renders this as at or above the top of the 2-4 h/day window, which INCLUDES 4 h. At the one value that matters for the claim's whole point — the top of the window — the paraphrase says the opposite of the quote's definition. (4) ASSOCIATION RESTATED AS HARM. The quote's verb is was associated with the occurrence of, an association from observational studies. The claim twice recasts it causally and evaluatively: the harm threshold ... was set at and the pooled harm estimate. Calling >4 h a harm threshold further implies the review identified 4 h as the point at which risk turns; the quote presents substantial as a prespecified exposure-category label, not an inflection point the analysis located. Both the causal hedge and the categorised exposure label scope condition are dropped. Defects (1)-(3) are the load-bearing i.e. clause — the only part of the claim doing interpretive work in a standing-desk argument — and none of it is in the quoted text.

refuted.claim: The exposure contrast in this trial was posture, not ambulation: the sitting reduction converted almost entirely into standing, with minimal change in light or moderate-to-vigorous physical activity in both arms — so the null cardiometabolic result at 24 months is a de facto posture-isolated null at a ~37 min/day standing dose.
refuted.why: The supporting quote IS verbatim page text (confirmed in the Results section: Both study arms observed reductions in sitting largely translated into standing behaviors and changes in LPA and MVPA activity were minimal.). But it does not license the claim as stated. Four specific defects: (1) STATES A NUMBER THE QUOTE DOES NOT STATE, AND MISATTRIBUTES IT. The quote contains zero numbers. ~37 min/day standing dose is imported from a different paragraph, where it is arm-specific and unit-specific: The adjusted within-arm mean difference in standing time for STAND + was ... 37.2 (21.8, 52.6) mins per 8 h workday relative to baseline. The adjusted within-arm mean difference in standing time in MOVE + was ... 24.4 (6.8, 41.9) mins per 8 h workday relative to baseline. The claim says in both arms and then attaches a single ~37 figure — that is STAND+'s number only; the other arm's was 24.4, ~34% lower. It also converts mins per 8 h workday into min/day, a unit swap the paper explicitly distinguishes (it reports workplace-time and total-waking-time variables as separate outcome sets). (2) THE QUOTE SAYS NOTHING ABOUT CARDIOMETABOLIC OUTCOMES. The cited sentence is exclusively about behavioral variables (sitting, standing, LPA, MVPA). The claim's entire payload — the null cardiometabolic result at 24 months is a de facto posture-isolated null — rests on a proposition absent from the quoted text. (3) DROPS A SCOPE CONDITION THE SOURCE CARRIES. The paper's cardiometabolic result is not a flat null: There were no significant changes in cardiometabolic risk within the total sample, while there were some significant changes in triglycerides and blood pressure for the dysglycemic participants — specifically a significant reduction in triglycerides for STAND+ from 12 to 24 months, and for MOVE+ from 0 to 24 months there were reductions in triglycerides and diastolic blood pressure. The authors further hedge the null as a power problem: A larger sample size is needed to detect concomitant impact on cardiometabolic health. The null cardiometabolic result strips both the subgroup exception and the underpowering caveat. (4) STRENGTHENS THE QUOTE'S HEDGE. Quote: largely translated into standing. Claim: converted almost entirely into standing. For MOVE+ the arithmetic is sitting -31.8 vs. standing +24.4 min/8 h workday (~77%), which largely covers and almost entirely does not — yet the claim asserts it for both arms. Counter-source for all four: the same article, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11978190/ (Results, Table-2 narrative paragraph; Abstract Results/Conclusions; Discussion paragraph beginning Minimal effects were seen in cardiometabolic risk factors).

refuted.claim: At 24 months this trial found no statistically significant cardiometabolic benefit in the full analytic sample (STAND+ n=175, MOVE+ n=149); the only significant biomarker movements were triglycerides and blood pressure inside a small exploratory dysglycemic subgroup (n=43 and n=27). Individual STAND+ total-sample point estimates fell below common MCIDs — systolic BP -2.0 mmHg (95% CI -4.1 to 0.2), diastolic BP -0.6 (-1.8 to 0.5), fasting glucose -1.9 mg/dL (-4.8 to 0.9).
refuted.why: Quote-support fails on two counts, one fatal. (1) SCOPE DROP / OVERGENERALIZATION CONTRADICTED BY THE SAME PAGE. The supporting quote is verbatim abstract text, but no significant changes in cardiometabolic risk within the total sample refers to the CMR composite Z-score, not to every biomarker. The claim converts it into a blanket no statistically significant cardiometabolic benefit in the full analytic sample plus the only significant biomarker movements were triglycerides and blood pressure inside a small exploratory dysglycemic subgroup (n=43 and n=27). Table 3 of the very same article contradicts that: MOVE+ Total (n=149), 0-24 months, Systolic BP -3.6 (-5.7, -1.6) mm Hg and Diastolic BP -2.3 (-3.4, -1.2) mm Hg — both CIs exclude zero, i.e. statistically significant BP reductions in the FULL analytic sample, not only the subgroup. Also in the total sample, MOVE+ fasting insulin 12-24 months is 9.5 (3.5, 15.5), another CI excluding zero. And the only significant... were triglycerides and blood pressure is wrong even inside the subgroup: STAND+ dysglycemic LDL-cholesterol 0-24 months is -8.3 (-16.0, -0.7). Counter-source is the cited page itself, Table 3 (Intervention effects on cardiometabolic risk biomarkers of the 24-month analytical sample by study arm). (2) NUMBERS ABSENT FROM THE QUOTE. The supporting quote states no sample sizes and no effect estimates. Every figure in the claim (n=175, n=149, n=43, n=27; SBP -2.0 [-4.1, 0.2]; DBP -0.6 [-1.8, 0.5]; glucose -1.9 [-4.8, 0.9]) comes from Table 3, not the quoted sentence. Those STAND+ values and subgroup n's do check out verbatim against Table 3, so this is a provenance defect rather than fabrication — but the claim is presented as resting on a quote that licenses none of it. Note also an internal inconsistency the claim inherits silently: the Results text says CMR score data were available for 175 and 150 STAND+ and MOVE+ participants, while Table 3 heads the MOVE+ column Total (n=149). (3) UNSOURCED EVALUATIVE ADDITION. fell below common MCIDs appears nowhere in the article; no MCID benchmark is stated or cited by the source. That judgment is the claim author's, presented as the source's finding. Defect 1 alone is disqualifying: the claim asserts the absence of a significant total-sample effect that the cited table reports as significant.

refuted.claim: The design cannot isolate the desk from the behavior-change bundle: both arms received the same multilevel intervention (organizational, environmental, social and individual components delivered by trained worksite advocates) and there was no non-intervention control group, so the observed sitting/standing changes cannot be attributed to the sit-stand workstation alone.
refuted.why: QUOTE-SUPPORT FAILURE (two distinct defects). (1) The quote covers one clause and licenses none of the rest. Verbatim page text offered is only: Some limitations worth noting include the lack of a non-intervention control group, limiting our ability to compare our results to worksites with no intervention. That single sentence supports ONLY there was no non-intervention control group. Everything else asserted in the claim is absent from the quote: that both arms received the same multilevel intervention, the enumerated bundle (organizational, environmental, social and individual components), delivered by trained worksite advocates, and the causal conclusion cannot be attributed to the sit-stand workstation alone. Those propositions do exist elsewhere on the page (Methods: MOVE+, the same multilevel intervention, however with SSW delivery at the end of the 12-month primary assessment period; the social-ecological organizational/policy... environmental... social... individual list; Worksites were responsible for identifying employee(s) to serve as advocate(s)... received training and monthly calls) — but they are NOT in the quote presented as support. The citation as filed is a stitched claim carrying one sentence of cover; a reader auditing the quote cannot verify ~80% of the claim from it. (2) The claim inverts the scope condition the quote actually carries. The quote's stated limitation is directional and narrow: inability to compare to worksites with NO intervention — i.e., the BUNDLE's effect versus nothing is unidentified. The claim silently repurposes this into the opposite inferential gap — that the DESK's effect within the bundle is unidentified. The paper's own design refutes that transposition: the arms differed only in SSW timing (STAND+ SSWs at baseline, MOVE+ SSWs deferred to after the 12-month primary assessment), which is precisely a randomized isolation of the incremental SSW effect over 0-12 months against an identical behavioral bundle. The paper flags loss of between-group comparability only for the LATER window: because of the differences between the STAND+ and MOVE+ intervention groups from 12- to 24-months (i.e., delayed intervention), we were unable to examine between group differences — a 12-24 month scope condition the claim drops entirely while presenting the limitation as global to the trial's sitting/standing findings. Net: the quote is verbatim but under-supports the claim as stated, and the inference drawn (cannot isolate the desk from the behavior-change bundle) is not the limitation the quoted sentence states. Correct restatement the quote WOULD license: the trial had no non-intervention control, so the multilevel intervention's total effect cannot be compared against worksites receiving nothing.

refuted.claim: As of the January 2019 search, no included study reported discomfort outcomes for physical-work-environment interventions (sit-stand or treadmill workstations) at medium term (6 to <12 months) or long term (>=12 months) — i.e. there was zero direct evidence on sit-stand desk musculoskeletal comfort at or beyond 6 months.
refuted.why: VERBATIM CHECK PASSES, GLOSS FAILS. I retrieved the full structured abstract of the cited review (PMID 31742666, DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD012487.pub2, Parry et al., Workplace interventions for increasing standing or walking for decreasing musculoskeletal symptoms in sedentary workers, e-pub 2019-11-17). The supporting quote is verbatim page text, it does sit inside the Physical work environment paragraph right after the sit-stand short-term results, and up to January 2019 is the stated search cut-off. So the first half of the claim (no included study reported discomfort outcomes ... at medium or long term) is licensed. THE EXACT OVERREACH is the i.e. clause: there was zero direct evidence on sit-stand desk musculoskeletal comfort at or beyond 6 months. The quote is scoped to ONE outcome family — discomfort outcomes — and the claim silently widens it to all musculoskeletal comfort evidence at >=6 months. The very next sentence of the same paragraph refutes the widened version: No significant reduction in pain-related disability was noted when a sit-stand workstation was used compared to when no intervention was provided in the medium term (mean difference (MD) -0.4, 95% CI -2.70 to 1.90; 1 RCT; low-quality evidence). There WAS direct sit-stand-workstation evidence at medium term (>=6 months) in this very review — one RCT on pain-related disability, which the review's own SELECTION CRITERIA list as a primary outcome (the impact of musculoskeletal symptoms such as pain-related disability). Zero direct evidence ... at or beyond 6 months is therefore contradicted by the source sentence immediately adjacent to the supporting quote. SECONDARY DEFECTS (same lens): (a) the claim converts a review-inclusion absence (no included study, inside eligibility limited to RCT/cluster-RCT/quasi-RCT/CBA designs in workers with musculoskeletal symptoms, 10 studies, n=955) into an unqualified statement about the state of evidence in the world; (b) the parenthetical (sit-stand or treadmill workstations) is imported from a different sentence in Main Results — the quoted sentence itself names no intervention, and the surrounding results text is sit-stand-specific, so attaching treadmill to the quote is not licensed by the quote; (c) discomfort is silently re-labelled musculoskeletal comfort, which is what lets the pain-related-disability counter-evidence get hidden. COUNTER-SOURCE: the same page/abstract, Main Results, Physical work environment paragraph, sentence following the supporting quote (verified via NCBI E-utilities efetch for PMID 31742666; cochranelibrary.com returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch).
